Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. PROPOSITION 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment and Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live
in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from
income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s
wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the
things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is
home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of
these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology
companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government
spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is
for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also
supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who
were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to
5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to
spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions,
and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to
spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The
rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain
amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect
tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections
would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is
very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires
would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock
prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all
those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires
may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example,
some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the
state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than
$1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the
account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how
much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of
dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires
equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from
billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax
revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
• Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue
collected from billionaires.

Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several

in income tax revenue from billionaires.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Californians vote on nation’s first wealth tax on billionaires

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 

If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. 

Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment and Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live
in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from
income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s
wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the
things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is
home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of
these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology
companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government
spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is
for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also
supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who
were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to
5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to
spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions,
and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to
spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The
rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain
amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect
tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections
would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is
very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires
would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock
prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all
those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires
may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example,
some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the
state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than
$1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the
account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how
much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of
dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires
equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from
billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax
revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
• Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue
collected from billionaires.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several
years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year
in income tax revenue from billionaires.

They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Californians vote on nation’s first wealth tax on billionaires

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 

If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. 

Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment and Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live
in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from
income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s
wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the
things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is
home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of
these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology
companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government
spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is
for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also
supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who
were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to
5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to
spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions,
and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to
spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The
rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain
amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect
tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections
would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is
very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires
would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock
prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all
those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires
may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example,
some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the
state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than
$1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the
account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how
much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of
dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires
equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from
billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax
revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
• Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue
collected from billionaires.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several
years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year
in income tax revenue from billionaires.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.
As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/20/nx-s1-5935597/california-billionaires-wealth-tax-sergey-brin) California since the tax was proposed.
Sponsor Message
On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) and podcast (https://www.npr.org/2019/07/24/744962126/episode-929-could-a-wealth-tax-work)). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires (https://gabriel-zucman.eu/we-need-to-tax-billionaires/). Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.
"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money .
On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.
Sponsor Message
" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."
It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html) in The New York Times .
A golden opportunity in the Golden State?
The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.
A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. That said, most of the wealth held by California billionaires is in publicly traded stocks, whose value is easy to determine.
Zucman, together with Jasper Boll and Emmanuel Saez, released an analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) of the California billionaire class and this proposed wealth tax.
Sponsor Message
"California billionaires' wealth has reached $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, as large as all the annual income reported on income tax returns of all Californians," they wrote. They found that California billionaire wealth had exploded by 144% between 2023 and 2025, thanks largely to the AI boom. "Over the longer run, the real wealth of California's billionaire class — the top 0.001% richest households — has been multiplied by 25 from 1982 to 2026, while average real family income in California has only doubled."
Zucman says a crucial problem with the existing tax system in California, America, and beyond is that the superrich have been seeing their wealth snowball bigger and bigger while paying relatively little in income taxes. Billionaires can structure their finances to generate little or no taxable income, making the income tax rate "totally irrelevant," he argues. Zucman believes a wealth tax will help address this, thereby helping to fight rising inequality, counteract the political power of "the oligarchs," and raise much-needed funds for everyone else.
Zucman, Boll, and Saez estimated that the state wealth tax proposed by Prop 40 could raise "about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax revenue." They arrive at that figure by taking 5% of their $2.3 trillion estimate of billionaire wealth, then reducing the projected revenue by 10% to account for avoidance, evasion, and the possibility that some billionaires ended their California residency before January 1, 2026.
Rauh argues that this 10% reduction to account for billionaires avoiding the tax is too optimistic.
Why past wealth taxes have been "abject failures"
As we've previously reported (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/newsletter/money), wealth taxes have been tried before around the world and they have had a dismal track record. Even Zucman, a wealth tax champion, writes in his new book that past wealth taxes "by and large, have been abject failures."
Zucman and his coterie of other (typically French) economists have spent a lot of time studying why past wealth taxes failed and have sought to design new ones that address those failures.
Sponsor Message
One crucial problem was that wealth taxes tended to have loopholes that allowed the rich to shelter their assets, making these taxes a leaky bucket. For example, before France scrapped its wealth tax back in 2018 (https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/11415-PGP.html/identifiant%3DACTU-2018-00087?utm_source=chatgpt.com), it exempted qualifying business assets, including shares in companies their owners ran. That, Zucman says, was a big loophole that drastically reduced the amount of revenue it raised.
Another crucial problem — which is at the center of the debate on this California wealth tax proposal — is that some superrich people move to avoid the tax. France became a cautionary tale, with critics often pointing to estimates that tens of thousands (https://www.mediapart.fr/en/journal/france/090815/rising-number-wealthy-french-fleeing-abroad?utm_source=chatgpt.com) of millionaires left while its wealth tax was in place. However, how much of that exodus was caused by the wealth tax remains disputed.
Zucman acknowledges that the flight of rich people has been an issue with past wealth taxes, but he also argues that this problem has been overblown. He, for example, pointed to a recent working paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35854?utm_source=chatgpt.com) about Norway, which has had a wealth tax since 1892 (https://www.reuters.com/business/norways-wealth-tax-trades-millionaires-equality-2025-11-24/). It found that recent increases to this existing wealth tax, alongside other tax increases on the rich, drove at most 100 rich people to leave. But, it found, those departures didn't do much to dent the resulting gains in wealth-tax revenue. That said, Norway is a nation, not a state, and moving to another country is a bigger deal than, say, moving from California to Nevada.
To avoid the failures of past wealth taxes, Prop 40's designers have tried to plug potential leaks. Unlike France's old wealth tax, it would tax business holdings, including shares in companies that billionaires run. And by making it a one-time, retroactive tax tied to where billionaires lived on January 1, 2026, they hope to prevent billionaires from escaping the bill by simply moving away.
Sponsor Message
However, whether these provisions will actually work is at the heart of the debate.
Are Prop 40 supporters just California Dreamin'?
Rauh recently released a competing analysis with a provocative conclusion: instead of raising $100 billion, as Zucman and the measure's supporters claim, this wealth tax could ultimately cost the state billions.
First, Rauh argues, at least seven famous billionaires had already left California before the January 1, 2026, residency cutoff, putting their fortunes beyond the tax's reach. Those billionaires are Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, and David Sacks.
Those departures alone, Rauh says, reduced the potential revenue from this wealth tax by "around $30 billion."
Zucman, however, disputes that those fortunes are beyond California's reach. He says the legal experts he trusts (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/podcast-episode/professor-brian-galle-how-to-tax-the-ultrarich-voices-carry/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) believe it's unlikely that any of these billionaires successfully ended their California tax residency before the cutoff. Ending your residency, he argues, takes more than a last-minute move across state lines. Prop 40 was designed with this in mind. It was announced in late October 2025 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-40-one?utm_source=chatgpt.com), giving billionaires only about two months to establish residency elsewhere before January 1, 2026. Talk about a New Year's Day hangover.
Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Sure, he's moved just across the border to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe — and meanwhile spent more than a hundred million dollars (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-138201/california-billionaire-tax-google-sergey-brin) trying to defeat Prop 40. But, Zucman says, he still frequently commutes to work in Silicon Valley. A quick change of address, he argues, doesn't necessarily mean you've left California behind for tax purposes. Rauh counters that Brin, backed by what we can only assume are the best accountants and lawyers, has likely succeeded in establishing Nevada residency. He stands by his assumption that Brin and the others are beyond the tax's reach.
Like much of the debate over how much this tax will ultimately raise, this dispute has as much to do with the law as it does economics.
Sponsor Message
Which leads us to the second reason Rauh believes this proposed wealth tax will raise much less money than its supporters hope: the courts. Billionaires, armed with the best lawyers money can buy, will mount a slew of constitutional challenges to this tax. And given this wealth tax's novelty — and the Supreme Court's conservative majority — there's a real risk that at least part of Prop 40 could be struck down.
For example, Prop 40's controversial retroactive provision. It would tax some billionaires based on where they used to live. Rauh argues that could violate the Constitution's due process protections, although the Supreme Court has upheld other retroactive taxes (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/512/26/) in the past. The tax also reaches beyond California's borders, targeting wealth held around the world, which could create legal issues. Rauh also raises legal concerns about how the tax would value privately held companies. He says that venture capital deals can put a price on a company that overstates what it's actually worth. Taxing an owner's share of that inflated value, he argues, could create constitutional problems.
The architects of Prop 40 designed the law with legal challenges in mind, and it has all sorts of fallback provisions meant to keep the tax working if the courts strike down any part of it. But how much revenue would survive those legal battles? This is another big disagreement between Rauh and Zucman.
Rauh and Jaros estimate a big range of possible outcomes. But their central estimate, which has generated plenty of headlines, cuts the remaining projected revenue in half to account for legal uncertainty. That is a strong assumption — not a certainty about how the courts will rule — and Zucman disputes it.
After accounting for billionaire departures and the anticipated legal challenges, Rauh and Jaros estimate the wealth tax would bring in only "around $30 billion."
Sponsor Message
But that's not the end of their gloomy estimate. Because Rauh and Jaros expect even more billionaires to flee the state if Prop 40 passes, taking their existing income tax payments with them.

Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.
As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/20/nx-s1-5935597/california-billionaires-wealth-tax-sergey-brin) California since the tax was proposed.
Sponsor Message
On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) and podcast (https://www.npr.org/2019/07/24/744962126/episode-929-could-a-wealth-tax-work)). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires (https://gabriel-zucman.eu/we-need-to-tax-billionaires/). Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.
"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money .
On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.
Sponsor Message
" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."
It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html) in The New York Times .
A golden opportunity in the Golden State?
The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.
A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. That said, most of the wealth held by California billionaires is in publicly traded stocks, whose value is easy to determine.
Zucman, together with Jasper Boll and Emmanuel Saez, released an analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) of the California billionaire class and this proposed wealth tax.
Sponsor Message
"California billionaires' wealth has reached $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, as large as all the annual income reported on income tax returns of all Californians," they wrote. They found that California billionaire wealth had exploded by 144% between 2023 and 2025, thanks largely to the AI boom. "Over the longer run, the real wealth of California's billionaire class — the top 0.001% richest households — has been multiplied by 25 from 1982 to 2026, while average real family income in California has only doubled."
Zucman says a crucial problem with the existing tax system in California, America, and beyond is that the superrich have been seeing their wealth snowball bigger and bigger while paying relatively little in income taxes. Billionaires can structure their finances to generate little or no taxable income, making the income tax rate "totally irrelevant," he argues. Zucman believes a wealth tax will help address this, thereby helping to fight rising inequality, counteract the political power of "the oligarchs," and raise much-needed funds for everyone else.
Zucman, Boll, and Saez estimated that the state wealth tax proposed by Prop 40 could raise "about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax revenue." They arrive at that figure by taking 5% of their $2.3 trillion estimate of billionaire wealth, then reducing the projected revenue by 10% to account for avoidance, evasion, and the possibility that some billionaires ended their California residency before January 1, 2026.
Rauh argues that this 10% reduction to account for billionaires avoiding the tax is too optimistic.
Why past wealth taxes have been "abject failures"
As we've previously reported (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/newsletter/money), wealth taxes have been tried before around the world and they have had a dismal track record. Even Zucman, a wealth tax champion, writes in his new book that past wealth taxes "by and large, have been abject failures."
Zucman and his coterie of other (typically French) economists have spent a lot of time studying why past wealth taxes failed and have sought to design new ones that address those failures.
Sponsor Message
One crucial problem was that wealth taxes tended to have loopholes that allowed the rich to shelter their assets, making these taxes a leaky bucket. For example, before France scrapped its wealth tax back in 2018 (https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/11415-PGP.html/identifiant%3DACTU-2018-00087?utm_source=chatgpt.com), it exempted qualifying business assets, including shares in companies their owners ran. That, Zucman says, was a big loophole that drastically reduced the amount of revenue it raised.
Another crucial problem — which is at the center of the debate on this California wealth tax proposal — is that some superrich people move to avoid the tax. France became a cautionary tale, with critics often pointing to estimates that tens of thousands (https://www.mediapart.fr/en/journal/france/090815/rising-number-wealthy-french-fleeing-abroad?utm_source=chatgpt.com) of millionaires left while its wealth tax was in place. However, how much of that exodus was caused by the wealth tax remains disputed.
Zucman acknowledges that the flight of rich people has been an issue with past wealth taxes, but he also argues that this problem has been overblown. He, for example, pointed to a recent working paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35854?utm_source=chatgpt.com) about Norway, which has had a wealth tax since 1892 (https://www.reuters.com/business/norways-wealth-tax-trades-millionaires-equality-2025-11-24/). It found that recent increases to this existing wealth tax, alongside other tax increases on the rich, drove at most 100 rich people to leave. But, it found, those departures didn't do much to dent the resulting gains in wealth-tax revenue. That said, Norway is a nation, not a state, and moving to another country is a bigger deal than, say, moving from California to Nevada.
To avoid the failures of past wealth taxes, Prop 40's designers have tried to plug potential leaks. Unlike France's old wealth tax, it would tax business holdings, including shares in companies that billionaires run. And by making it a one-time, retroactive tax tied to where billionaires lived on January 1, 2026, they hope to prevent billionaires from escaping the bill by simply moving away.
Sponsor Message
However, whether these provisions will actually work is at the heart of the debate.
Are Prop 40 supporters just California Dreamin'?
Rauh recently released a competing analysis with a provocative conclusion: instead of raising $100 billion, as Zucman and the measure's supporters claim, this wealth tax could ultimately cost the state billions.
First, Rauh argues, at least seven famous billionaires had already left California before the January 1, 2026, residency cutoff, putting their fortunes beyond the tax's reach. Those billionaires are Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, and David Sacks.
Those departures alone, Rauh says, reduced the potential revenue from this wealth tax by "around $30 billion."
Zucman, however, disputes that those fortunes are beyond California's reach. He says the legal experts he trusts (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/podcast-episode/professor-brian-galle-how-to-tax-the-ultrarich-voices-carry/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) believe it's unlikely that any of these billionaires successfully ended their California tax residency before the cutoff. Ending your residency, he argues, takes more than a last-minute move across state lines. Prop 40 was designed with this in mind. It was announced in late October 2025 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-40-one?utm_source=chatgpt.com), giving billionaires only about two months to establish residency elsewhere before January 1, 2026. Talk about a New Year's Day hangover.
Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Sure, he's moved just across the border to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe — and meanwhile spent more than a hundred million dollars (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-138201/california-billionaire-tax-google-sergey-brin) trying to defeat Prop 40. But, Zucman says, he still frequently commutes to work in Silicon Valley. A quick change of address, he argues, doesn't necessarily mean you've left California behind for tax purposes. Rauh counters that Brin, backed by what we can only assume are the best accountants and lawyers, has likely succeeded in establishing Nevada residency. He stands by his assumption that Brin and the others are beyond the tax's reach.
Like much of the debate over how much this tax will ultimately raise, this dispute has as much to do with the law as it does economics.
Sponsor Message
Which leads us to the second reason Rauh believes this proposed wealth tax will raise much less money than its supporters hope: the courts. Billionaires, armed with the best lawyers money can buy, will mount a slew of constitutional challenges to this tax. And given this wealth tax's novelty — and the Supreme Court's conservative majority — there's a real risk that at least part of Prop 40 could be struck down.
For example, Prop 40's controversial retroactive provision. It would tax some billionaires based on where they used to live. Rauh argues that could violate the Constitution's due process protections, although the Supreme Court has upheld other retroactive taxes (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/512/26/) in the past. The tax also reaches beyond California's borders, targeting wealth held around the world, which could create legal issues. Rauh also raises legal concerns about how the tax would value privately held companies. He says that venture capital deals can put a price on a company that overstates what it's actually worth. Taxing an owner's share of that inflated value, he argues, could create constitutional problems.
The architects of Prop 40 designed the law with legal challenges in mind, and it has all sorts of fallback provisions meant to keep the tax working if the courts strike down any part of it. But how much revenue would survive those legal battles? This is another big disagreement between Rauh and Zucman.
Rauh and Jaros estimate a big range of possible outcomes. But their central estimate, which has generated plenty of headlines, cuts the remaining projected revenue in half to account for legal uncertainty. That is a strong assumption — not a certainty about how the courts will rule — and Zucman disputes it.
After accounting for billionaire departures and the anticipated legal challenges, Rauh and Jaros estimate the wealth tax would bring in only "around $30 billion."
Sponsor Message
But that's not the end of their gloomy estimate. Because Rauh and Jaros expect even more billionaires to flee the state if Prop 40 passes, taking their existing income tax payments with them.
