New Analysis: Proposition 40 Could Raise Billions, but Poses Serious Tradeoffs
Report Also Examines How Propositions 41 and 42 Could Limit Prop. 40 and Future Measures
August 4, 2026 | By Kyra Moeller (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kyra-moeller/) and Mauricio Torres Jr. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/mauricio-torres/)
SACRAMENTO, CA — A new publication (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) from the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) (Budget Center) examines Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, and what it could mean for California’s budget, public services, and long-term fiscal outlook.
The analysis finds Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) — a first-in-the-nation 5% tax on the wealth of California’s roughly 250 billionaires, who hold a combined $2 trillion — could generate tens of billions in one-time revenue to help offset deep federal funding cuts to health care, food assistance, and education. But because the proposal is unprecedented at the state level, the report cautions that the funding is temporary, does not support other vital public services or address Californians’ broader affordability challenges, and notes concerns about its unknown long-term economic impacts.
“California is facing difficult choices as federal funding cuts hurt Californians’ ability to access health care, food assistance, and other vital programs,” said Chris Hoene , executive director of the California Budget & Policy Center. “Our analysis shows how Proposition 40 could potentially generate substantial one-time revenue to help offset cuts to some services, while also examining the very real uncertainties and tradeoffs that come with implementing a novel tax.”
The report explains that California is expected to lose tens of billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal alone, and that approximately 1.3 million Californians are projected to lose health coverage by 2029-30 under recent policy changes in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 would dedicate 90% of the revenue raised to health care and the remaining 10% would be split among education and food assistance.
Budget Center policy experts examine key questions surrounding anticipated legal challenges and location decisions by billionaires. The report argues there is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth in the Golden State, given growing wealth inequality, new federal tax cuts, and the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth. However, because a wealth tax is untested at a state level in the United States, it carries real uncertainty. Courts may strike down the measure or portions of it and conflicting measures could lead to years of litigation.
Because the tax is untested, estimates of how much revenue it would generate vary widely, and no one can say how billionaires’ location decisions might change or what that would mean for California’s economy and finances long-term.
“California needs additional revenue to support the well-being of its residents and offset the deeply harmful federal cuts,” added Hoene . “Voters will have to decide if the significant risks of Prop. 40 are worth the gamble, or if they’ll instead look to their legislative leaders to raise revenues through other sources next session.”
The analysis also examines Propositions 41 and 42, which seek to block the state’s ability to tax wealth, including invalidating Prop. 40, or impose significant administrative and procedural hurdles that would effectively produce the same result.
To view the full publication and additional budget measure analyses, visit calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/) .

Under California's constitution, when measures that conflict pass at the same election, the one with the most yes votes prevails, so I'm working through how that applies to Prop 40

I'm checking how Prop 40's conflict clause works against Props 41 and 42: it prevails only if it gets more yes votes than each conflicting measure. Since the user is asking about a yes vote on 40, I'm weighing whether 41 or 42 could end up overriding it.

I'm noting that a Yes on 40 could still be cancelled by 41 or 42 if either gets more yes votes. I'm now looking at international evidence on wealth taxes, including the Norway study that found roughly 100 wealthy people left, and Swiss and Swedish migration research showing modest but larger responses among the very rich. I'm considering whether to search for more of this evidence base.

I'm now checking the international evidence on wealth taxes, looking at mobility responses in Switzerland, Sweden, and Norway, since that's where the Zucman and Rauh debate really hinges. I'm now checking whether the Legislature or Newsom has put forward an alternative to Prop 40, and I'm also weighing how the spending on the opposing side compares to the measure's own committee.

I'm checking the retirement account provisions in more detail: Roth accounts above $10 million look taxable, which is a real nuance against the claim that retirement savings are untouched. I'm checking whether the statutory tax rate and the $1B threshold could be changed by a two-thirds legislative vote, since they sit in statute rather than the constitution. A CalMatters lawyer thinks the lower threshold would probably be blocked, because the purpose language centers on billionaires, so that's a legal question I'd want to check.

Now I'm checking how the Prop 98 school funding claim holds up, and whether the measure's revenue would be counted against the Gann limit, since the text says it isn't treated as appropriations subject to that limit.

I'm checking the Gann limit angle now: the opponents claim the measure exempts its revenue from the spending cap, which would bypass the rule that excess revenue be split between schools and taxpayer rebates. I also want to see whether the revenue gets counted against the required budget reserve deposits under Prop 2.

I'm weighing the decision on values and facts: whether taxing billionaires' wealth is worth it, how much Medi-Cal funding is at stake, and the risks of migration, legal challenges, drafting problems, and interactions with Props 41 and 42. I'm also starting to look at the revenue estimates, which vary widely.

I'm weighing the revenue estimates: proponents suggest $100B or more, the Stanford work points to around $30B after departures and litigation, and the LAO's "tens of billions" seems to sit between those, which makes the official figure look closer to the lower estimates. I'm also noting that the LAO's income tax revenue loss is under $1 billion a year, while the Rauh and Jaros figures run higher.

I'm comparing the income tax loss estimates: the LAO puts it under $1 billion a year, while Boll, Saez, and Zucman call it comparatively minor, with billionaires paying about $3.2 billion in state income tax. Rauh and Jaros run higher, between $1 and $3.5 billion a year. I'm also noting that the measure's spending is mostly directed at health, so it would act as a one-time buffer against federal Medi-Cal cuts rather than a lasting fix.

I'm weighing whether the $30 billion total would be used up quickly, since at the $22.5 billion-a-year appropriation cap it would cover only about a year and a half of the federal Medi-Cal cuts. That makes the measure look more like a short-term buffer than a lasting fix for an ongoing gap.

I'm checking the legal risk next: the measure has an expedited validation path straight to the Supreme Court and a severability clause, and Rauh thinks parts could still be struck down. The retroactive, residency-based wealth reach raises novel constitutional questions, though courts have generally upheld retroactive taxes before.

I'm looking at the measure's design now: it includes a five-year installment option with a steep 7.5% annual deferral charge and a 5% withholding rule for out-of-state assets, which seems aimed at easing liquidity problems. I'm noting that the measure puts 90% of its revenue toward health care with a non-supplant rule, but it also exempts itself from the Prop 98 school funding guarantee, so that money wouldn't count toward the roughly 40% of General Fund revenue that goes to schools.

I'm weighing the case for Yes: the measure would raise a substantial one-time sum, plausibly tens of billions, to offset federal Medi-Cal cuts that run far larger each year.

I'm also checking the LAO's estimate that the income tax loss stays under $1 billion a year, and noting that past ballot measures of this kind have had mixed outcomes.

I'm also considering the risk that around 30% of the billionaire base has already left, which is disputed, along with the broader threat of capital flight and damage to the startup ecosystem.

I'm weighing the legal and governance risks now: the measure's novel constitutional questions, the chance that a validation challenge strikes parts of it and drags out uncertainty, and the debate over whether the two-thirds legislative amendment clause could reach beyond billionaires. I'm also looking at public finance concerns, since the measure sits outside Prop 98, the Gann limit, and reserve rules, and the opponents' claim of a few billion a year lost to schools still needs checking.

I'm now looking at how the measure's sponsor and competing measures could affect the outcome, since Props 41 and 42 could nullify it even with a yes majority. The sponsor's conduct has also drawn allegations and litigation, which adds another layer of uncertainty.

I'm weighing whether to mention the sponsor's allegations, which the union denies. They aren't about the measure's policy merits, so I'd keep any mention brief and neutral. The user wants a yes or no, but the evidence on outcomes is mixed, so I'll give a recommendation and be clear that it's a judgment call.

I'm working through a rough revenue range for Prop 40: somewhere around $30 to $60 billion once departures, litigation, and valuation issues are factored in, with the money likely arriving over 2027 to 2031 through the installment schedule.

I'm weighing the remaining points: the measure's revenue could plausibly stretch only a few years against roughly $19 billion a year in federal Medi-Cal cuts, so it works as a bridge rather than a fix. I'm also judging the economic side, where the tax is a one-time hit that might push some departures, with an estimated income tax loss of around $1 to $3.5 billion a year against a state budget above $300 billion.

I'm now looking at the academic evidence on how wealthy people respond to wealth taxes at the subnational level, such as Swiss cantons, where the tax differences seem to drive the very rich to move. New Analysis: Proposition 40 Could Raise Billions, but Poses Serious Tradeoffs
Report Also Examines How Propositions 41 and 42 Could Limit Prop. 40 and Future Measures
August 4, 2026 | By Kyra Moeller (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kyra-moeller/) and Mauricio Torres Jr. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/mauricio-torres/)
SACRAMENTO, CA — A new publication (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) from the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) (Budget Center) examines Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, and what it could mean for California’s budget, public services, and long-term fiscal outlook.
The analysis finds Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) — a first-in-the-nation 5% tax on the wealth of California’s roughly 250 billionaires, who hold a combined $2 trillion — could generate tens of billions in one-time revenue to help offset deep federal funding cuts to health care, food assistance, and education. But because the proposal is unprecedented at the state level, the report cautions that the funding is temporary, does not support other vital public services or address Californians’ broader affordability challenges, and notes concerns about its unknown long-term economic impacts.
“California is facing difficult choices as federal funding cuts hurt Californians’ ability to access health care, food assistance, and other vital programs,” said Chris Hoene , executive director of the California Budget & Policy Center. “Our analysis shows how Proposition 40 could potentially generate substantial one-time revenue to help offset cuts to some services, while also examining the very real uncertainties and tradeoffs that come with implementing a novel tax.”
The report explains that California is expected to lose tens of billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal alone, and that approximately 1.3 million Californians are projected to lose health coverage by 2029-30 under recent policy changes in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 would dedicate 90% of the revenue raised to health care and the remaining 10% would be split among education and food assistance.
Budget Center policy experts examine key questions surrounding anticipated legal challenges and location decisions by billionaires. The report argues there is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth in the Golden State, given growing wealth inequality, new federal tax cuts, and the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth. However, because a wealth tax is untested at a state level in the United States, it carries real uncertainty. Courts may strike down the measure or portions of it and conflicting measures could lead to years of litigation.
Because the tax is untested, estimates of how much revenue it would generate vary widely, and no one can say how billionaires’ location decisions might change or what that would mean for California’s economy and finances long-term.
“California needs additional revenue to support the well-being of its residents and offset the deeply harmful federal cuts,” added Hoene . “Voters will have to decide if the significant risks of Prop. 40 are worth the gamble, or if they’ll instead look to their legislative leaders to raise revenues through other sources next session.”
The analysis also examines Propositions 41 and 42, which seek to block the state’s ability to tax wealth, including invalidating Prop. 40, or impose significant administrative and procedural hurdles that would effectively produce the same result.
To view the full publication and additional budget measure analyses, visit calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/) .

40 includes language exempting its revenues from the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues.
If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers.
^2^ Because a 5% tax on California’s billionaires would most likely push state revenues over the Gann Limit, this exemption would be critical to directing all of Prop.
40’s revenues to healthcare and food assistance.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenues.

Press Release
New Analysis: Proposition 40 Could Raise Billions, but Poses Serious Tradeoffs
Report Also Examines How Propositions 41 and 42 Could Limit Prop. 40 and Future Measures
August 4, 2026 | By Kyra Moeller (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kyra-moeller/) and Mauricio Torres Jr. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/mauricio-torres/)
SACRAMENTO, CA — A new publication (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) from the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) (Budget Center) examines Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, and what it could mean for California’s budget, public services, and long-term fiscal outlook.
The analysis finds Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) — a first-in-the-nation 5% tax on the wealth of California’s roughly 250 billionaires, who hold a combined $2 trillion — could generate tens of billions in one-time revenue to help offset deep federal funding cuts to health care, food assistance, and education. But because the proposal is unprecedented at the state level, the report cautions that the funding is temporary, does not support other vital public services or address Californians’ broader affordability challenges, and notes concerns about its unknown long-term economic impacts.
“California is facing difficult choices as federal funding cuts hurt Californians’ ability to access health care, food assistance, and other vital programs,” said Chris Hoene , executive director of the California Budget & Policy Center. “Our analysis shows how Proposition 40 could potentially generate substantial one-time revenue to help offset cuts to some services, while also examining the very real uncertainties and tradeoffs that come with implementing a novel tax.”
The report explains that California is expected to lose tens of billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal alone, and that approximately 1.3 million Californians are projected to lose health coverage by 2029-30 under recent policy changes in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 would dedicate 90% of the revenue raised to health care and the remaining 10% would be split among education and food assistance.
Budget Center policy experts examine key questions surrounding anticipated legal challenges and location decisions by billionaires. The report argues there is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth in the Golden State, given growing wealth inequality, new federal tax cuts, and the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth. However, because a wealth tax is untested at a state level in the United States, it carries real uncertainty. Courts may strike down the measure or portions of it and conflicting measures could lead to years of litigation.
Because the tax is untested, estimates of how much revenue it would generate vary widely, and no one can say how billionaires’ location decisions might change or what that would mean for California’s economy and finances long-term.
“California needs additional revenue to support the well-being of its residents and offset the deeply harmful federal cuts,” added Hoene . “Voters will have to decide if the significant risks of Prop. 40 are worth the gamble, or if they’ll instead look to their legislative leaders to raise revenues through other sources next session.”
The analysis also examines Propositions 41 and 42, which seek to block the state’s ability to tax wealth, including invalidating Prop. 40, or impose significant administrative and procedural hurdles that would effectively produce the same result.
To view the full publication and additional budget measure analyses, visit calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/) .

Marius Brülhart, Jonathan Gruber, Matthias Krapf & Kurt Schmidheiny
Working Paper 22376
DOI 10.3386/w22376

We study the effects of wealth taxation on reported wealth.
Our analysis is based on data for Switzerland, which has the highest rate of annual wealth taxation in the developed world.

We use aggregate data on wealth holdings by canton and individual-level data for the canton of Bern.
Our estimated behavioral elasticities substantially exceed those of the taxable income literature.

# Does A Progressive Wealth Tax Reduce Top Wealth Inequality? Evidence From Switzerland
**Authors: Samira Marti, Isabel Z. Martínez and Florian Scheuer**
Like in many other countries, wealth inequality has increased in Switzerland over the last fifty years.
By providing new evidence on cantonal top wealth shares for each of the 26 cantons since 1969, we show that the overall trend masks striking differences across cantons, both in levels and trends.
Combining this with variation in cantonal wealth taxes, we then estimate an event study model to identify the dynamic effects of reforms to top wealth tax rates on the subsequent evolution of wealth concentration.
Our results imply that a reduction in the top marginal wealth tax rate by 0.1 percentage points increases the top 1% (0.1%) wealth share by 0.9 (1.2) percentage points five years after the reform.
This suggests that wealth tax cuts over the last 50 years explain roughly 18% (25%) of the increase in wealth concentration among the top 1% (0.1%).

Marius Brülhart, Jonathan Gruber, Matthias Krapf & Kurt Schmidheiny
Working Paper 22376
DOI 10.3386/w22376
Issue Date June 2016
We study the effects of wealth taxation on reported wealth.
Our analysis is based on data for Switzerland, which has the highest rate of annual wealth taxation in the developed world.
While the wealth tax base is defined at the federal level, tax rates vary considerably across locations and over time.
We use aggregate data on wealth holdings by canton and individual-level data for the canton of Bern.
Our estimated behavioral elasticities substantially exceed those of the taxable income literature.
We also find that taxpayers bunch below the tax threshold, that observed responses are driven by changes in wealth holdings rather than mobility, and that financial wealth is somewhat more responsive than non-financial wealth.

# What Switzerland can teach us on the pros and cons of wealth taxes
In a recent study (Brülhart et al. 2019), we study taxable wealth by canton over the period 2003-2015.
Since this was a period of multiple canton-level tax reforms, we can track aggregate responses of wealth holdings to rich longitudinal variation in wealth tax levels.
We find that reported wealth holdings in Switzerland are very responsive to wealth taxation.
Figure 1 shows how log taxable wealth in a canton evolves in response to a drop in the wealth tax rate.

Marius Brülhart, Jonathan Gruber, Matthias Krapf & Kurt Schmidheiny

We study the effects of wealth taxation on reported wealth.
Our analysis is based on data for Switzerland, which has the highest rate of annual wealth taxation in the developed world.

We use aggregate data on wealth holdings by canton and individual-level data for the canton of Bern.
Our estimated behavioral elasticities substantially exceed those of the taxable income literature.

# Does A Progressive Wealth Tax Reduce Top Wealth Inequality? Evidence From Switzerland
**Authors: Samira Marti, Isabel Z. Martínez and Florian Scheuer**
Like in many other countries, wealth inequality has increased in Switzerland over the last fifty years.
By providing new evidence on cantonal top wealth shares for each of the 26 cantons since 1969, we show that the overall trend masks striking differences across cantons, both in levels and trends.
Combining this with variation in cantonal wealth taxes, we then estimate an event study model to identify the dynamic effects of reforms to top wealth tax rates on the subsequent evolution of wealth concentration.
Our results imply that a reduction in the top marginal wealth tax rate by 0.1 percentage points increases the top 1% (0.1%) wealth share by 0.9 (1.2) percentage points five years after the reform.
This suggests that wealth tax cuts over the last 50 years explain roughly 18% (25%) of the increase in wealth concentration among the top 1% (0.1%).

Marius Brülhart, Jonathan Gruber, Matthias Krapf & Kurt Schmidheiny
Working Paper 22376
DOI 10.3386/w22376
Issue Date June 2016
We study the effects of wealth taxation on reported wealth.
Our analysis is based on data for Switzerland, which has the highest rate of annual wealth taxation in the developed world.
While the wealth tax base is defined at the federal level, tax rates vary considerably across locations and over time.
We use aggregate data on wealth holdings by canton and individual-level data for the canton of Bern.
Our estimated behavioral elasticities substantially exceed those of the taxable income literature.
We also find that taxpayers bunch below the tax threshold, that observed responses are driven by changes in wealth holdings rather than mobility, and that financial wealth is somewhat more responsive than non-financial wealth.

# Does A Progressive Wealth Tax Reduce Top Wealth Inequality? Evidence From Switzerland
**Authors: Samira Marti, Isabel Z. Martínez and Florian Scheuer**
Like in many other countries, wealth inequality has increased in Switzerland over the last fifty years.
By providing new evidence on cantonal top wealth shares for each of the 26 cantons since 1969, we show that the overall trend masks striking differences across cantons, both in levels and trends.
Combining this with variation in cantonal wealth taxes, we then estimate an event study model to identify the dynamic effects of reforms to top wealth tax rates on the subsequent evolution of wealth concentration.
Our results imply that a reduction in the top marginal wealth tax rate by 0.1 percentage points increases the top 1% (0.1%) wealth share by 0.9 (1.2) percentage points five years after the reform.
This suggests that wealth tax cuts over the last 50 years explain roughly 18% (25%) of the increase in wealth concentration among the top 1% (0.1%).

Billionaire Tax Act
September 14, 2026
Prepared by
the Blue Sky Consulting Group
Page 1
Contents

The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue .................................................. 2

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of BTA Expenditures .................................................................................... 5

Fiscal Impact of BTA Expenditures ........................................................................................................ 7
Potential Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Billionaire Departures ............................................................... 7
Billionaires Are Unlikely to Leave (or Return to) California Due to the BTA’s Approval (or Rejection) ......... 8
Quantitative Analysis of Prospective Mobility Losses Under the BTA ....................................................... 9
No Evidence of Business Investment Losses Following BTA’s Filing .................................................... 9
Estimation of Upper-Bound Mobility Loss Under the BTA .................................................................. 11
Conclusion ............................................................................................................................................ 14
Appendix – Fiscal Impact Estimate Methodology ..................................................................................... 15
Personal Income Tax (PIT)................................................................................................................... 15
PIT from Employees ........................................................................................................................ 15
PIT from Proprietor Employment ..................................................................................................... 15
Pass-Through Income from S-Corps ................................................................................................ 16
Corporate Income Tax ........................................................................................................................ 16
Sales and Use Tax .............................................................................................................................. 16
Acknowledgements
This report was prepared by James Paci, Shawn Blosser, and Matthew Newman for the Service Employees
International Union – United Healthcare Workers West. The analysis presented and the conclusions of this
report are those of the authors.
Page 2
Executive Summary
The Billionaire Tax Act (“BTA”) would assess a one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, generating
an estimated $116 billion in revenue for the State of California, or $23.2 billion annually for five years.1 Over
this period, the expenditure of wealth tax revenues is estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary
jobs in California annually—including nearly 150,000 direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and
education sectors—and $45.7 billion in annual economic output. This activity would in turn generate, in
addition to the direct wealth tax revenue, an estimated $1.4 billion annually in personal income,
corporation and sales tax revenue for the state and local governments.
Available data suggest that the measure's filing has not affected California’s business climate (contrary to
claims made by the BTA’s opponents): across measures of early-stage investment, total venture capital
funding, and business formation, the state’s share of national activity has held steady or increased since
the measure’s introduction in October 2025. Moreover, even under aggressive assumptions regarding the
responsiveness of California’s billionaires to the BTA’s one-time wealth tax, revenue losses attributable to
the potential departures of some of the state’s billionaires are modest relative to the revenues raised by the
measure.
Estimation of Wealth Tax Revenue Generated by the BTA
The BTA would assess a one-time 5% tax on the total net worth, excluding directly held real estate, of
billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For
purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be
valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).
The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue
According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List (the “Forbes List”), as of August 15, 2026, California was
home to 261 billionaires who together held a collective net worth of approximately $2.34 trillion.2 As a
result, after excluding the share of this wealth comprised of directly held real estate (an estimated 0.6% of
total net worth),3 the BTA’s one-time 5% wealth tax would generate an estimated $116.2 billion to fund BTA
initiatives. Because the BTA allows billionaire taxpayers to spread their tax liability over five equal annual
installments, it is expected that expenditures of wealth tax revenue will also be distributed over a five-year
period. Therefore, this report’s estimates of the BTA’s annual economic and fiscal impacts reflect an
estimated $23.2 billion of BTA expenditures annually (i.e., $116.2 billion divided by five years).
1 The BTA allows individuals subject to the wealth tax to spread their total tax liability over five annual installments.
2 Forbes, “Real-Time Billionaires List,” accessed August 17, 2026. Estimates of the combined net worth of the
individuals on the Forbes List who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026, are adopted from the “California
Billionaire Wealth Tracker” (accessed August 17, 2026), which serves as an exhibit to Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez, and
Gabriel Zucman, “California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates,” NBER Working Paper
35218 (July 2026).
3 The BTA exempts directly held real estate, pensions, retirement accounts, and personal property held outside of
California. To account for these exemptions, the actual tax basis used here is $2.325 trillion, reflecting a 0.6%
discount attributable to real estate’s estimated share of total billionaire net worth, following the approach outlined in
Joshua Rauh, Benjamin Jaros, Gregory Kearney, John Doran, and Matheus Cosso, “The Net Present Value of the
Billionaire Tax Act,” Hoover Institution, March 5, 2026.
Page 3
Sensitivity of Revenue Estimate to Billionaire Undercounting and Tax
Avoidance
Due to uncertainty regarding the potential underestimation of billionaire net worth, the undercounting of
billionaire residents of California, and billionaires’ avoidance of the tax through changes in residency, the
baseline estimate of the total billionaire net worth subject to the wealth tax (i.e., $2.34 trillion as of August
15, 2026) may understate or overstate the actual tax base.
Underestimates of net worth and undercounting of billionaires – The estimated number and wealth of
California’s billionaires used in this report are based on the Forbes List. While Forbes provides the only
publicly available data source identifying all taxpayers potentially subject to the BTA, a recent comparison
of Forbes’ and Bloomberg’s ranking of the 500 richest people notes that, due to differing methodologies for
estimating net worth, Bloomberg’s net worth estimates for California’s billionaires are, on average, 7.5%
higher than Forbes’ estimates.4
Separately, statistical analysis of the distribution of Forbes List billionaires by Boll et al. (2026) suggests
that the list excludes many billionaires with net worths of less than $5 billion. If the estimated combined net
worth of these “missing” billionaires is included in the BTA’s estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue would
increase by $24.6 billion (or 21.2% of the baseline).5
Together, these two adjustments to Forbes’ net worth estimates would combine to generate a 30.2%
increase in the wealth tax base above the baseline estimate.6
Wealth tax avoidance – Because the wealth tax is imposed only on individuals who were California
residents as of the measure’s January 1, 2026, tax obligation date, the BTA could raise less than $116 billion
if some of the state’s billionaires established nonresidency, for state tax law purposes, prior to this date.
Since the measure’s filing in October 2025, news reports have identified five California billionaires who took
steps to relocate to other states prior to January 1, 2026; these individuals account for roughly $588 billion
of the $2.34 trillion of total California billionaire net worth, or approximately $29.2 billion of future wealth
tax revenue.7 Additionally, some observers have noted that the wealth tax could be deemed a “retroactive”
tax prohibited by the United States Constitution. If such a challenge were successful, a court could
effectively shift the tax obligation date to Election Day, resulting in a further reduction of wealth tax
4 Brian Galle, David Gamage, Emmanuel Saez, and Darien Shanske, “Expert Report On The California 2026 Billionaire
Tax: Revenue, Economic, and Constitutional Analysis,” July 20, 2026. The “Bloomberg Billionaire Index” estimates only
the net worths of the world’s 500 richest people but does not specifically identify California billionaires.
5 Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) at 20. The authors note that while the distribution of individual net worths in the
Forbes List closely matches a Pareto distribution for net worths greater than $4.5 billion, the ranking departs from this
expected distribution below this wealth threshold (where billionaires are relatively less visible and therefore more
likely not to be identified by Forbes). Based on extrapolation of the Pareto distribution to values between $1 billion and
$4.5 billion, Boll et al. estimate that, as of July 1, 2026, roughly 368 California billionaires with a combined net worth of
$615 billion are missing from the Forbes List (or 26.7% of the total $2.307 trillion of net worth held by Forbes-identified
billionaires as of that date). To estimate wealth tax revenues from these billionaires, Boll et al. discount this combined
net worth by 20% to account for higher expected levels of tax avoidance from these less visible billionaires. As a result,
these individuals’ effective total tax base is an estimated $492 billion ($615 billion * (1 – 0.2)) and generates $24.6
billion of wealth tax revenue (5% of $492 billion).
6 The individual percentage increases are compounding, such that the total percentage increase is equal to
((1+0.075)*(1+0.212)-1).
7 The list of potential pre-January 1, 2026, billionaire departures is based on Rauh et al. (2026), and includes Larry
Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, and Steven Spielberg. (Rauh et al. also include David Sacks in their list of
pre-obligation departures but as of August 15, 2026, Sacks is no longer listed on Forbes’ billionaires list.)
Page 4
revenue.8 News reports have identified four billionaires with a combined net worth of $218 billion—
equivalent to $10.8 billion of wealth tax revenue—who announced California departures after January 1,
2026.9
However, given the difficulty of establishing non-residency under California tax law, the impact of these
reported departures on wealth tax revenue is highly uncertain. A taxpayer’s California residency depends on
a wide-ranging assessment of the taxpayer’s connection to the state during the relevant tax period, and
taxpayers bear the burden of establishing that they have “substantially severed” their connections to
California. In making this determination, the Franchise Tax Board (FTB) considers the totality of a taxpayer’s
connections to the state, evaluating factors such as physical presence, the location of family members,
professional and business relationships, and property holdings, among other factors.10
Based on reports published since the BTA’s filing, three of the five billionaires who announced departures
before January 1, 2026 (Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and Peter Thiel), as well as one of the four reported post-
January 1 departers (Mark Zuckerberg), have retained relevant connections to California.11 This group
collectively accounts for 95% of the $807 billion of total net worth held by all nine individuals who have left
the state.
Figure 1 shows wealth tax revenue estimates under various assumptions as to the total California billionaire
tax base and billionaire tax avoidance. If none of the state’s billionaires avoid the tax by establishing non-
residency, the BTA would generate $116.2 billion of revenue based only on the Forbes-estimated net worth
of billionaires identified by Forbes as of August 15, 2026 (i.e., the baseline revenue estimate). If the total
estimated net worth of missing billionaires is added to the Forbes-estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue
8 The proponents of the BTA have argued that retroactivity going back to the year of the tax is constitutional under
existing Supreme Court law; see for example David Gamage, Brian D. Galle, and Darien Shanske, "Correcting the
Record: Responding to Some Legal Arguments About the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act," January 2, 2026. Opponents’
arguments are presented in Baker Botts, “California 2026 Billionaire Tax Act,” December 15, 2025. The Blue Sky
Consulting Group expresses no opinion on the merits of these legal arguments but addresses them here for the sake of
completeness, recognizing that a thorough assessment of potential revenue impact outcomes should account for the
full range of scenarios.
9 The list of potential post-January 1, 2026, billionaire departures is based on Rauh et al. (2026) and includes Mark
Zuckerberg, Jan Koum, Reed Hastings, and Andy Fang. Since that study’s publication, news reports have not identified
any additional departures.
10 State of California Franchise Tax Board (FTB), “Residency and Sourcing Technical Manual,” (Rev. 11/2022).
11 Larry Page reportedly purchased two properties in Florida just prior to January 1, 2026, but “appear[ed] to still own
two homes in Palo Alto, California, worth around $33 million.” Forbes Wealth Team, “What proposed billionaire tax
could cost the world’s richest people,” January 16, 2026.
Sergey Brin reportedly purchased property in Nevada in December 2025, but Forbes reported in January 2026 that
Sergey Brin has “three kids in California and owns three properties across Los Altos and Malibu, worth roughly $57
million.” Forbes Wealth Team (January 16, 2026). In April, the New York Times reported that Brin was reportedly
spending “every other week at Google’s California headquarters, alternating with Nevada.” Theodore Schleifer and
Kate Conger, “Sergey Brin Moves to the Right, With a ‘MAGA Girlfriend’ by His Side,” April 27, 2026.
A New York Times article published five days prior to the January 1 tax obligation date notes that Peter Thiel was still
the owner of a home in Hollywood Hills and was “exploring” opening another office for his investment firm, Thiel
Capital, in Miami. Ryan Mac, Theodore Schleifer, and Heather Knight, “A Wealth Tax Floated in California Has
Billionaires Thinking of Leaving,” New York Times, December 26, 2025.
As of the date of this memorandum, Mark Zuckerberg owns an 11-home compound in Palo Alto, California and
continues to serve as the Chief Executive Officer at Meta. Queenie Wong, “Mark Zuckerberg Buys an Irish Castle,” Los
Angeles Times, August 22, 2026.
Page 5
increases to an estimated $140.8 billion (i.e., $116.2 billion plus $24.6 billion from the missing billionaires).
Finally, if the wealth tax base is further adjusted to reflect Bloomberg’s higher average net worth estimates,
the state would collect $151.4 billion (i.e., a 7.5% increase on $140.8 billion).
The state would collect less wealth tax revenue to the extent some billionaires are able to avoid the wealth
tax. The low-end revenue estimates in the final row of Figure 1 reflect the assumption that a court will move
the tax obligation date to Election Day and that, as a result, all nine identified departures are able to

departures).12 However, if missing billionaires are included and Bloomberg’s wealth adjustment is adopted,
estimated revenue increases to $108.3 billion.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of BTA Expenditures
The state’s expenditures of wealth tax revenue on health care, food assistance, and education programs
would generate a net increase in economic activity and employment statewide.
BTA Economic Impact Estimates
Because billionaire wealth is predominantly held in appreciating assets rather than converted into annual
consumption, the wealth tax would draw almost entirely on funds that would not otherwise have entered
the California economy. As a result, the net increase in spending on goods and services under the BTA is
approximately equal to the amount of wealth tax revenue raised each year.13
12 The nine departures collectively account for an estimated $806.5 billion of net worth (i.e., $588.2 billion from the
pre-January 1, 2026, departures and $218.3 billion from the four post-January 1 departures), or 34.5% of the $2.34
trillion held by all 261 identified California billionaires. If these individuals’ net worths were excluded entirely from the
BTA tax base, estimated wealth tax revenue declines by $40.1 billion (i.e., 34.5% of $116.2 billion).
13 Based on empirical research summarized in this report’s discussion of upper-bound billionaire tax revenue losses
(see “Tax Revenue Generated by Billionaires’ Personal Consumption,” page 12), it is estimated that only 2.15% of
billionaire net worth is earned as income annually, and only a fraction of this income is consumed in California (rather
than saved or spent outside the state). Further, most sales of shares (if any) required to pay BTA liabilities would come
from national and global investors, effectively placing this global revenue into circulation in the California economy.
Page 6
Of the estimated $23.2 billion generated by the BTA annually over five years under baseline assumptions, an
estimated 0.7% share, or $170 million, would cover BTA administrative costs such as tax enforcement.14
The BTA directs 90% of the remaining revenue, or $20.77 billion annually, to support health care services
and 10%, or $2.31 billion, to food assistance and education programs.15 These expenditures comprise the
“direct” economic effects of the measure. The recipients of direct spending (e.g., hospitals, schools)

Executive Summary
The Billionaire Tax Act (“BTA”) would assess a one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, generating
an estimated $116 billion in revenue for the State of California, or $23.2 billion annually for five years.1 Over
this period, the expenditure of wealth tax revenues is estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary
jobs in California annually—including nearly 150,000 direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and
education sectors—and $45.7 billion in annual economic output. This activity would in turn generate, in
addition to the direct wealth tax revenue, an estimated $1.4 billion annually in personal income,
corporation and sales tax revenue for the state and local governments.
Available data suggest that the measure's filing has not affected California’s business climate (contrary to
claims made by the BTA’s opponents): across measures of early-stage investment, total venture capital
funding, and business formation, the state’s share of national activity has held steady or increased since
the measure’s introduction in October 2025. Moreover, even under aggressive assumptions regarding the
responsiveness of California’s billionaires to the BTA’s one-time wealth tax, revenue losses attributable to
the potential departures of some of the state’s billionaires are modest relative to the revenues raised by the
measure.
Estimation of Wealth Tax Revenue Generated by the BTA
The BTA would assess a one-time 5% tax on the total net worth, excluding directly held real estate, of
billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For
purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be
valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).
The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue
According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List (the “Forbes List”), as of August 15, 2026, California was
home to 261 billionaires who together held a collective net worth of approximately $2.34 trillion.2 As a
result, after excluding the share of this wealth comprised of directly held real estate (an estimated 0.6% of
total net worth),3 the BTA’s one-time 5% wealth tax would generate an estimated $116.2 billion to fund BTA
initiatives. Because the BTA allows billionaire taxpayers to spread their tax liability over five equal annual
installments, it is expected that expenditures of wealth tax revenue will also be distributed over a five-year
period. Therefore, this report’s estimates of the BTA’s annual economic and fiscal impacts reflect an
estimated $23.2 billion of BTA expenditures annually (i.e., $116.2 billion divided by five years).

Sensitivity of Revenue Estimate to Billionaire Undercounting and Tax
Avoidance
Due to uncertainty regarding the potential underestimation of billionaire net worth, the undercounting of
billionaire residents of California, and billionaires’ avoidance of the tax through changes in residency, the
baseline estimate of the total billionaire net worth subject to the wealth tax (i.e., $2.34 trillion as of August
15, 2026) may understate or overstate the actual tax base.
Underestimates of net worth and undercounting of billionaires – The estimated number and wealth of
California’s billionaires used in this report are based on the Forbes List. While Forbes provides the only
publicly available data source identifying all taxpayers potentially subject to the BTA, a recent comparison
of Forbes’ and Bloomberg’s ranking of the 500 richest people notes that, due to differing methodologies for
estimating net worth, Bloomberg’s net worth estimates for California’s billionaires are, on average, 7.5%
higher than Forbes’ estimates.4
Separately, statistical analysis of the distribution of Forbes List billionaires by Boll et al. (2026) suggests
that the list excludes many billionaires with net worths of less than $5 billion. If the estimated combined net
worth of these “missing” billionaires is included in the BTA’s estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue would
increase by $24.6 billion (or 21.2% of the baseline).5

increase in the wealth tax base above the baseline estimate.6

residents as of the measure’s January 1, 2026, tax obligation date, the BTA could raise less than $116 billion

tax revenue.7 Additionally, some observers have noted that the wealth tax could be deemed a “retroactive”
tax prohibited by the United States Constitution. If such a challenge were successful, a court could
effectively shift the tax obligation date to Election Day, resulting in a further reduction of wealth tax

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of BTA Expenditures
The state’s expenditures of wealth tax revenue on health care, food assistance, and education programs
would generate a net increase in economic activity and employment statewide.
BTA Economic Impact Estimates
Because billionaire wealth is predominantly held in appreciating assets rather than converted into annual
consumption, the wealth tax would draw almost entirely on funds that would not otherwise have entered
the California economy. As a result, the net increase in spending on goods and services under the BTA is
approximately equal to the amount of wealth tax revenue raised each year.13

trillion held by all 261 identified California billionaires. If these individuals’ net worths were excluded entirely from the
BTA tax base, estimated wealth tax revenue declines by $40.1 billion (i.e., 34.5% of $116.2 billion).

Executive Summary
The Billionaire Tax Act (“BTA”) would assess a one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, generating
an estimated $116 billion in revenue for the State of California, or $23.2 billion annually for five years.1 Over
this period, the expenditure of wealth tax revenues is estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary
jobs in California annually—including nearly 150,000 direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and
education sectors—and $45.7 billion in annual economic output. This activity would in turn generate, in
addition to the direct wealth tax revenue, an estimated $1.4 billion annually in personal income,
corporation and sales tax revenue for the state and local governments.
Available data suggest that the measure's filing has not affected California’s business climate (contrary to
claims made by the BTA’s opponents): across measures of early-stage investment, total venture capital
funding, and business formation, the state’s share of national activity has held steady or increased since
the measure’s introduction in October 2025. Moreover, even under aggressive assumptions regarding the
responsiveness of California’s billionaires to the BTA’s one-time wealth tax, revenue losses attributable to
the potential departures of some of the state’s billionaires are modest relative to the revenues raised by the
measure.
Estimation of Wealth Tax Revenue Generated by the BTA
The BTA would assess a one-time 5% tax on the total net worth, excluding directly held real estate, of
billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For
purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be
valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).
The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue
According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List (the “Forbes List”), as of August 15, 2026, California was
home to 261 billionaires who together held a collective net worth of approximately $2.34 trillion.2 As a
result, after excluding the share of this wealth comprised of directly held real estate (an estimated 0.6% of
total net worth),3 the BTA’s one-time 5% wealth tax would generate an estimated $116.2 billion to fund BTA
initiatives. Because the BTA allows billionaire taxpayers to spread their tax liability over five equal annual
installments, it is expected that expenditures of wealth tax revenue will also be distributed over a five-year
period. Therefore, this report’s estimates of the BTA’s annual economic and fiscal impacts reflect an
estimated $23.2 billion of BTA expenditures annually (i.e., $116.2 billion divided by five years).

billionaire residents of California, and billionaires’ avoidance of the tax through changes in residency, the
baseline estimate of the total billionaire net worth subject to the wealth tax (i.e., $2.34 trillion as of August
15, 2026) may understate or overstate the actual tax base.
Underestimates of net worth and undercounting of billionaires – The estimated number and wealth of
California’s billionaires used in this report are based on the Forbes List. While Forbes provides the only
publicly available data source identifying all taxpayers potentially subject to the BTA, a recent comparison
of Forbes’ and Bloomberg’s ranking of the 500 richest people notes that, due to differing methodologies for
estimating net worth, Bloomberg’s net worth estimates for California’s billionaires are, on average, 7.5%
higher than Forbes’ estimates.4
Separately, statistical analysis of the distribution of Forbes List billionaires by Boll et al. (2026) suggests
that the list excludes many billionaires with net worths of less than $5 billion. If the estimated combined net
worth of these “missing” billionaires is included in the BTA’s estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue would
increase by $24.6 billion (or 21.2% of the baseline).5
Together, these two adjustments to Forbes’ net worth estimates would combine to generate a 30.2%
increase in the wealth tax base above the baseline estimate.6
Wealth tax avoidance – Because the wealth tax is imposed only on individuals who were California
residents as of the measure’s January 1, 2026, tax obligation date, the BTA could raise less than $116 billion
if some of the state’s billionaires established nonresidency, for state tax law purposes, prior to this date.

tax prohibited by the United States Constitution. If such a challenge were successful, a court could
effectively shift the tax obligation date to Election Day, resulting in a further reduction of wealth tax

However, given the difficulty of establishing non-residency under California tax law, the impact of these

billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For
purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be
valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).

I'm also weighing how Props 41 and 42 interact with that precedent risk, and then I'll look for the latest court or polling developments and Zucman's stated views on a one-time versus annual tax.

I'm noting that Zucman, in his book, favors an annual wealth tax and reportedly doesn't see this as a true one-time measure, so the "one-time" framing carries some tension with the sponsors' broader goals. Voters may read that differently: some as a reason to say no, others as a first step.

Prop
40
CA
Prop
40
|
Constitutional Amendment and Statute
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
Enacts a one-time state wealth tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with a net worth of more than $1 billion.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors did not reach consensus on Prop. 40.
The proposed tax would provide one-time funds to meet the urgent health care and food access needs of millions of vulnerable Californians. Because it only applies to the wealthiest individuals with the most ability to pay, it is a progressive tax. However, the proposal fails on some good government principles. The tax’s one-time revenue would not fund ongoing health care and food programs. The state will need a permanent solution to the gaps H.R. 1 creates, not just a one-time fix. Furthermore, it could cost the state hundreds of millions in long-term revenue if billionaires flee in response. Prop. 40 has failed to gain consensus among many unions and health care advocates concerned about these potential negative impacts.
Given strong policy arguments for and against the measure, SPUR is not making an endorsement.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 40 Would Do
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time excise tax of 5% on individuals with a net worth of at least $1.1 billion in 2027. For individuals or trusts with a net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would decrease by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million in net worth below $1.1 billion. 1 The net worth calculation would include publicly traded securities, private business entities, art, intellectual property, vehicles, personal property, grantor trust assets, and dependents’ assets that exceed $50,000. The tax would not apply to real estate, pensions, individual retirement savings, and Roth accounts with an aggregate value below $10 million. Taxpayers could spread their payments over five years, but they would have to pay more to do so.
The tax would apply to all billionaires with residence in California on or after January 1, 2026. Because the date is retroactive, it may be challenging for some taxpayers to evade it by moving.
For many billionaires, their sources of wealth include publicly traded stocks as well as shares of private companies. The tax measure would value public stock at market price as of December 31, 2026, and value private business entities based on book value, estimated profits, and percentage of ownership or voting rights. Taxpayers could appeal the methodology and submit their own appraisals of private assets, including privately owned businesses, art, and intellectual property.
Revenues from Prop. 40 would be restricted. The vast majority of the funds, 90%, would go to health care to address recent federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal and other social programs. The remaining 10% would go to food assistance and education programs. Prop. 40 would prohibit the state from cutting existing funding for these purposes.
Prop. 40 includes language exempting its revenues from the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 2 Because a 5% tax on California’s billionaires would most likely push state revenues over the Gann Limit, this exemption would be critical to directing all of Prop. 40’s revenues to healthcare and food assistance.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenues. However, the exact amount is difficult to calculate because net worth fluctuates and some billionaires may find ways to reduce their liability.
The Backstory
Federal bill H.R. 1, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” was enacted in July 2025 and will make heavy cuts to critical social safety net programs across the state, including about $19 billion in annual funding losses to Medi-Cal. Medi-Cal covers more than one-third of the state’s population, including half of children aged 0 to 5, and nearly 15 million low-income Californians. 3 Funding cuts are projected to accelerate hospital closures across California, particularly in rural areas. They are also expected to heavily impact food assistance programs such as CalFresh and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which serve an estimated 5 million Californians.
The funding cuts are occurring as income inequality in California is increasing. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the highest-income families in the 90th percentile earn 11 times as much as the lowest-income families in the 10th percentile. 4 In recent years, inflation has hit low-income families the hardest, and households are struggling to pay for essential goods and services such as food, housing, transportation, and health care. 5
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country, with the highest income brackets paying the highest effective tax rates. In 2012, voters approved Prop. 30, which implemented tax rate increases on high-income earners, starting at $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for married couples. Voters renewed this income tax structure with Prop. 55 in 2016, extending it to 2030. (This election’s California Prop. 3 would make that increase permanent.) Despite concerns that tax rate increases cause wealthy Californians to leave the state, studies have shown no evidence of such tax flight following previous income tax increases. Indeed, the state has lost lower-income and less-educated adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults. 6
SEIU-UHW, a public sector union representing health care workers, placed Prop. 40 on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort. The measure requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 40 would be a highly progressive tax, applying only to individuals with more than $1 billion in net worth. California’s nearly 250 billionaires hold more than $2 trillion in wealth, up 48% from 2025 to 2026. Yet billionaires pay about 24% of their income in taxes, compared with 30% for the average taxpayer, and less than 1.5% of their wealth annually in federal, state, and local taxes. 7
Additionally, the measure would address disparities in how Californians experience the tax system. Low-income families bear a disproportionate burden from high housing costs and regressive taxes such as property and sales taxes, while inherited wealth is not taxed in California, contributing to income inequality and persistent racial wealth disparities. 8
The revenue raised would overwhelmingly support lower-income Californians by funding Medi-Cal, food assistance, and public education. These benefits have a racial equity dimension: According to U.S. Census data, low-income families in California are much more likely to be Latino or Black, while most high-income families are white or Asian. Prop. 40 would therefore raise revenue exclusively from the state’s wealthiest residents while directing it to services disproportionately relied on by lower-income, Black, and Latino Californians.
Pros
Implementing the proposed tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue to mitigate the drastic federal funding cuts to healthcare, food assistance, and other services for low-income Californians, allowing many public and rural hospitals to remain open.
Revenues from the tax would disproportionately benefit low-income Californians who depend on Medi-Cal and SNAP benefits.
The highly progressive wealth tax would apply only to billionaires, who experienced enormous wealth gains last year. Because the tax is retroactive and one-time, it would be difficult for billionaires to evade.
Cons
Prop. 40 would fill a budget deficit with one-time funds and would not address the structural deficit left by federal funding cuts.
A potential exodus of billionaires in protest could reduce personal income tax revenue over time, a major ongoing source of state revenue.
California already has the highest income tax rate in the United States, and a new tax on private assets could strengthen the perception that the state is not a competitive location for individuals and companies.
No Recommendation

40
CA
Prop
40
|
Constitutional Amendment and Statute
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
Enacts a one-time state wealth tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with a net worth of more than $1 billion.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors did not reach consensus on Prop. 40.
The proposed tax would provide one-time funds to meet the urgent health care and food access needs of millions of vulnerable Californians. Because it only applies to the wealthiest individuals with the most ability to pay, it is a progressive tax. However, the proposal fails on some good government principles. The tax’s one-time revenue would not fund ongoing health care and food programs. The state will need a permanent solution to the gaps H.R. 1 creates, not just a one-time fix. Furthermore, it could cost the state hundreds of millions in long-term revenue if billionaires flee in response. Prop. 40 has failed to gain consensus among many unions and health care advocates concerned about these potential negative impacts.
Given strong policy arguments for and against the measure, SPUR is not making an endorsement.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 40 Would Do
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time excise tax of 5% on individuals with a net worth of at least $1.1 billion in 2027. For individuals or trusts with a net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would decrease by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million in net worth below $1.1 billion. 1 The net worth calculation would include publicly traded securities, private business entities, art, intellectual property, vehicles, personal property, grantor trust assets, and dependents’ assets that exceed $50,000. The tax would not apply to real estate, pensions, individual retirement savings, and Roth accounts with an aggregate value below $10 million. Taxpayers could spread their payments over five years, but they would have to pay more to do so.
The tax would apply to all billionaires with residence in California on or after January 1, 2026. Because the date is retroactive, it may be challenging for some taxpayers to evade it by moving.
For many billionaires, their sources of wealth include publicly traded stocks as well as shares of private companies. The tax measure would value public stock at market price as of December 31, 2026, and value private business entities based on book value, estimated profits, and percentage of ownership or voting rights. Taxpayers could appeal the methodology and submit their own appraisals of private assets, including privately owned businesses, art, and intellectual property.
Revenues from Prop. 40 would be restricted. The vast majority of the funds, 90%, would go to health care to address recent federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal and other social programs. The remaining 10% would go to food assistance and education programs. Prop. 40 would prohibit the state from cutting existing funding for these purposes.
Prop. 40 includes language exempting its revenues from the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 2 Because a 5% tax on California’s billionaires would most likely push state revenues over the Gann Limit, this exemption would be critical to directing all of Prop. 40’s revenues to healthcare and food assistance.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenues. However, the exact amount is difficult to calculate because net worth fluctuates and some billionaires may find ways to reduce their liability.
The Backstory
Federal bill H.R. 1, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” was enacted in July 2025 and will make heavy cuts to critical social safety net programs across the state, including about $19 billion in annual funding losses to Medi-Cal. Medi-Cal covers more than one-third of the state’s population, including half of children aged 0 to 5, and nearly 15 million low-income Californians. 3 Funding cuts are projected to accelerate hospital closures across California, particularly in rural areas. They are also expected to heavily impact food assistance programs such as CalFresh and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which serve an estimated 5 million Californians.
The funding cuts are occurring as income inequality in California is increasing. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the highest-income families in the 90th percentile earn 11 times as much as the lowest-income families in the 10th percentile. 4 In recent years, inflation has hit low-income families the hardest, and households are struggling to pay for essential goods and services such as food, housing, transportation, and health care. 5
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country, with the highest income brackets paying the highest effective tax rates. In 2012, voters approved Prop. 30, which implemented tax rate increases on high-income earners, starting at $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for married couples. Voters renewed this income tax structure with Prop. 55 in 2016, extending it to 2030. (This election’s California Prop. 3 would make that increase permanent.) Despite concerns that tax rate increases cause wealthy Californians to leave the state, studies have shown no evidence of such tax flight following previous income tax increases. Indeed, the state has lost lower-income and less-educated adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults. 6
SEIU-UHW, a public sector union representing health care workers, placed Prop. 40 on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort. The measure requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 40 would be a highly progressive tax, applying only to individuals with more than $1 billion in net worth. California’s nearly 250 billionaires hold more than $2 trillion in wealth, up 48% from 2025 to 2026. Yet billionaires pay about 24% of their income in taxes, compared with 30% for the average taxpayer, and less than 1.5% of their wealth annually in federal, state, and local taxes. 7
Additionally, the measure would address disparities in how Californians experience the tax system. Low-income families bear a disproportionate burden from high housing costs and regressive taxes such as property and sales taxes, while inherited wealth is not taxed in California, contributing to income inequality and persistent racial wealth disparities. 8
The revenue raised would overwhelmingly support lower-income Californians by funding Medi-Cal, food assistance, and public education. These benefits have a racial equity dimension: According to U.S. Census data, low-income families in California are much more likely to be Latino or Black, while most high-income families are white or Asian. Prop. 40 would therefore raise revenue exclusively from the state’s wealthiest residents while directing it to services disproportionately relied on by lower-income, Black, and Latino Californians.
Pros
Implementing the proposed tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue to mitigate the drastic federal funding cuts to healthcare, food assistance, and other services for low-income Californians, allowing many public and rural hospitals to remain open.
Revenues from the tax would disproportionately benefit low-income Californians who depend on Medi-Cal and SNAP benefits.
The highly progressive wealth tax would apply only to billionaires, who experienced enormous wealth gains last year. Because the tax is retroactive and one-time, it would be difficult for billionaires to evade.
Cons
Prop. 40 would fill a budget deficit with one-time funds and would not address the structural deficit left by federal funding cuts.
A potential exodus of billionaires in protest could reduce personal income tax revenue over time, a major ongoing source of state revenue.
California already has the highest income tax rate in the United States, and a new tax on private assets could strengthen the perception that the state is not a competitive location for individuals and companies.

I'm noting that the Blue Sky report was prepared for the union that sponsored the measure, so its $116 billion figure comes from a proponent-commissioned analysis. The Berkeley economists' roughly $100 billion estimate is also aligned with the proponents, while the nonpartisan LAO only says "tens of billions." Now I'm turning to what else the Blue Sky report says.

Now I'm weighing the Blue Sky scenarios, which put revenue between $76B and $151B depending on the assumptions, against Rauh's $30B. The gap between them looks like it comes mainly from whether a 50% litigation discount is applied to the base.

The revenue estimate seems to hinge mostly on whether the measure survives legal challenges. If it largely does, revenue could land around $80–120B; if half the base is lost, closer to $30–50B. I'm also looking at the legal critiques: one says the retroactive residency date conflicts with Supreme Court precedent, while the proponents' experts see low facial-challenge risk, so there's a real expert dispute to present on both sides.

I'm comparing the income-tax loss figures: Blue Sky's upper bound of about $0.64B a year, Rauh's $1–3.5B a year, and the LAO's under $1B. The Blue Sky number sits below the LAO's ceiling, which makes the LAO figure look less like a strict upper limit.

I'm checking the revenue figures against each other: Rauh's NBER paper gives a net present value loss of about $38.9B, which is the most recent number, versus the earlier $25B in the Hoover press coverage. Working through the rough ranges now: if the ongoing losses are $0.6B to $3.5B a year, the net effect swings a lot with how many people actually leave and for how long. A low-departure case roughly breaks even against the $30B one-time figure, while a higher-departure case turns clearly negative.

I'm weighing the long-run fiscal side now: the revenue is likely large up front, but whether the state comes out ahead depends on how many billionaires leave and for how long, since the ongoing income-tax losses could be small or substantial.

Now I'm looking at the structural side: the one-time revenue would only bridge a few years of federal Medi-Cal cuts against an ongoing deficit, so it isn't a lasting fix. I'm also noting the design issues: Prop 98 exemption, constitutional entrenchment, and the oversight questions that Prop 41 tries to address.

I'm looking at the late-October polls now: support for Prop 40 has slipped to around 42–46%, with opposition from Newsom, the teachers' and doctors' associations, and business groups, though labor and the state Democratic Party are behind it. The bigger risk is Props 41 and 42, which could cancel the measure even if it wins, since 42 currently polls higher on yes votes than 40 does.

I'm weighing the case for a "no" recommendation: high legal and migration risk, uncertain and possibly temporary revenue, and built-in budget exemptions. I'm also setting it against the case for "yes": the state faces large federal health-care cuts, and the tax falls on a small group with low effective rates.

I'm weighing the revenue side: even the conservative estimates are sizable, and the residency cutoff should limit how many people leave. Both sides of the Prop 40 question have real weight, so this comes down to how much risk a voter is willing to accept.

I'm running the expected-value math on the revenue: at around $50B after a litigation haircut, spread over five years, that's roughly $10B a year, a few percent of the general fund but a meaningful slice of health spending. I'm setting that against the departure, legal, and entrenchment risks I've already listed.

I'm weighing the expected value now: even with a 20–30% chance the measure is struck down or narrowed, the fiscal math still looks positive under LAO-style assumptions, with departure losses offsetting only a modest share of the revenue. The budget uncertainty from pending litigation and the non-fiscal costs, like capital flight and governance changes, are the parts that could tip it the other way.

I'm now weighing the case for "No" on the mobility point: wealthy people do respond to wealth taxes, and moving between states is easier than moving abroad, so departures could be larger than in national examples. Polling has also softened, with many Democrats opposed.

I'm now setting out the points for "Yes": the tax lands on a few hundred very wealthy people, the health care gap is real, and the revenue, even at pessimistic estimates, is large next to the immediate shortfall. I'm also noting that the design tries to block avoidance with a January 1 residency date, a valuation date, and global wealth counting.

I'm also noting that the measure is one-time rather than an annual wealth tax, which limits ongoing burdens, though the "No" case rests on how uncertain the court outcome and billionaire behavior are.

I'm settling on "No" as my recommendation, but I'm treating it as a judgment call: the revenue case hinges on contested numbers and court outcomes.
