Constitutional Amendment and Statute
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
Enacts a one-time state wealth tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with a net worth of more than $1 billion.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors did not reach consensus on Prop. 40.
The proposed tax would provide one-time funds to meet the urgent health care and food access needs of millions of vulnerable Californians. Because it only applies to the wealthiest individuals with the most ability to pay, it is a progressive tax. However, the proposal fails on some good government principles. The tax’s one-time revenue would not fund ongoing health care and food programs. The state will need a permanent solution to the gaps H.R. 1 creates, not just a one-time fix. Furthermore, it could cost the state hundreds of millions in long-term revenue if billionaires flee in response. Prop. 40 has failed to gain consensus among many unions and health care advocates concerned about these potential negative impacts.
Given strong policy arguments for and against the measure, SPUR is not making an endorsement.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 40 Would Do
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time excise tax of 5% on individuals with a net worth of at least $1.1 billion in 2027. For individuals or trusts with a net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would decrease by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million in net worth below $1.1 billion. 1 The net worth calculation would include publicly traded securities, private business entities, art, intellectual property, vehicles, personal property, grantor trust assets, and dependents’ assets that exceed $50,000. The tax would not apply to real estate, pensions, individual retirement savings, and Roth accounts with an aggregate value below $10 million. Taxpayers could spread their payments over five years, but they would have to pay more to do so.
The tax would apply to all billionaires with residence in California on or after January 1, 2026. Because the date is retroactive, it may be challenging for some taxpayers to evade it by moving.
For many billionaires, their sources of wealth include publicly traded stocks as well as shares of private companies. The tax measure would value public stock at market price as of December 31, 2026, and value private business entities based on book value, estimated profits, and percentage of ownership or voting rights. Taxpayers could appeal the methodology and submit their own appraisals of private assets, including privately owned businesses, art, and intellectual property.
Revenues from Prop. 40 would be restricted. The vast majority of the funds, 90%, would go to health care to address recent federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal and other social programs. The remaining 10% would go to food assistance and education programs. Prop. 40 would prohibit the state from cutting existing funding for these purposes.
Prop. 40 includes language exempting its revenues from the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 2 Because a 5% tax on California’s billionaires would most likely push state revenues over the Gann Limit, this exemption would be critical to directing all of Prop. 40’s revenues to healthcare and food assistance.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenues. However, the exact amount is difficult to calculate because net worth fluctuates and some billionaires may find ways to reduce their liability.
The Backstory
Federal bill H.R. 1, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” was enacted in July 2025 and will make heavy cuts to critical social safety net programs across the state, including about $19 billion in annual funding losses to Medi-Cal. Medi-Cal covers more than one-third of the state’s population, including half of children aged 0 to 5, and nearly 15 million low-income Californians. 3 Funding cuts are projected to accelerate hospital closures across California, particularly in rural areas. They are also expected to heavily impact food assistance programs such as CalFresh and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which serve an estimated 5 million Californians.
The funding cuts are occurring as income inequality in California is increasing. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the highest-income families in the 90th percentile earn 11 times as much as the lowest-income families in the 10th percentile. 4 In recent years, inflation has hit low-income families the hardest, and households are struggling to pay for essential goods and services such as food, housing, transportation, and health care. 5
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country, with the highest income brackets paying the highest effective tax rates. In 2012, voters approved Prop. 30, which implemented tax rate increases on high-income earners, starting at $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for married couples. Voters renewed this income tax structure with Prop. 55 in 2016, extending it to 2030. (This election’s California Prop. 3 would make that increase permanent.) Despite concerns that tax rate increases cause wealthy Californians to leave the state, studies have shown no evidence of such tax flight following previous income tax increases. Indeed, the state has lost lower-income and less-educated adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults. 6
SEIU-UHW, a public sector union representing health care workers, placed Prop. 40 on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort. The measure requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 40 would be a highly progressive tax, applying only to individuals with more than $1 billion in net worth. California’s nearly 250 billionaires hold more than $2 trillion in wealth, up 48% from 2025 to 2026. Yet billionaires pay about 24% of their income in taxes, compared with 30% for the average taxpayer, and less than 1.5% of their wealth annually in federal, state, and local taxes. 7
Additionally, the measure would address disparities in how Californians experience the tax system. Low-income families bear a disproportionate burden from high housing costs and regressive taxes such as property and sales taxes, while inherited wealth is not taxed in California, contributing to income inequality and persistent racial wealth disparities. 8
The revenue raised would overwhelmingly support lower-income Californians by funding Medi-Cal, food assistance, and public education. These benefits have a racial equity dimension: According to U.S. Census data, low-income families in California are much more likely to be Latino or Black, while most high-income families are white or Asian. Prop. 40 would therefore raise revenue exclusively from the state’s wealthiest residents while directing it to services disproportionately relied on by lower-income, Black, and Latino Californians.
Pros
Implementing the proposed tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue to mitigate the drastic federal funding cuts to healthcare, food assistance, and other services for low-income Californians, allowing many public and rural hospitals to remain open.
Revenues from the tax would disproportionately benefit low-income Californians who depend on Medi-Cal and SNAP benefits.
The highly progressive wealth tax would apply only to billionaires, who experienced enormous wealth gains last year. Because the tax is retroactive and one-time, it would be difficult for billionaires to evade.
Cons
Prop. 40 would fill a budget deficit with one-time funds and would not address the structural deficit left by federal funding cuts.
A potential exodus of billionaires in protest could reduce personal income tax revenue over time, a major ongoing source of state revenue.
California already has the highest income tax rate in the United States, and a new tax on private assets could strengthen the perception that the state is not a competitive location for individuals and companies.

The latest article is dated Nov 3, 2026, so today is probably election day, and the vote on this measure is happening now or about to. SPUR, a nonpartisan urban policy group, said its board could not agree on Prop 40 and made no recommendation, which is worth noting even for an organization that generally favors more housing.

I'm noting that SPUR's board split and gave no recommendation, and that its concerns center on the measure's one-time funding and the risk of wealthy residents leaving. The Gann limit exemption is the key tension: proponents see it as necessary to direct all revenue to health care, while opponents say it skips the rebate and school allocation rules. That comes down to a values question.

I'm checking the Prop 41 and 42 polling against Prop 40, since a Yes vote on 40 could be nullified if either of those gets more yes votes. Props 41 and 42 both contain that nullification clause, and the late-October PPIC poll had Prop 42 ahead of Prop 40, which matters for a Yes voter.

Next I'm checking the expert critiques on the legal side: a Gupta Wessler risk assessment that rates facial challenges as low-risk, against the Tax Foundation's view that the measure faces many constitutional challenges and that its retroactive residency date is fatally flawed. I'm also noting Zucman's position that Prop 40 may be a first step toward an annual wealth tax, and the critique that Hoover's NPV estimates count the loss from fear of future taxes but not the gains.

I'm weighing the Medi-Cal angle now: the measure's health account can cover restoring federal cuts or protecting Medi-Cal, but the Legislature would decide how and when that money gets spent, so nothing guarantees it reaches Medi-Cal specifically.

I'm weighing the Legislature's room to amend the measure later: a two-thirds vote in each house could change it, and Democrats hold supermajorities in both chambers, though any amendment would still have to be consistent with and further the measure's purposes.

I'm checking whether Democrats really hold two-thirds of the seats in both houses, since that bears on how easily the Legislature could amend the measure later. From what I recall, they hold about 60 of 80 Assembly seats and 30 of 40 Senate seats, but I want to confirm those numbers before relying on them.

I'm thinking about whether the 2/3 threshold matters if Democrats already hold supermajorities, since that would let them amend the measure without Republican votes. I want to check the current seat counts before I rely on that, and I'm also weighing the measure's startup valuation rule, which sets a floor at the last funding round and could leave founders with illiquid wealth facing a tax bill they can't easily pay.

I'm looking at the startup valuation issue: the Rauh critique says the deferral protections are inadequate, while Zucman's team argues the optional deferral account handles liquidity problems for founders. Then I'm checking whether the measure's health spending could simply cover general Medi-Cal costs instead of new coverage, though the "restore reductions" and "not supplant" language seems to limit that.

I'm weighing the fiscal side now, looking at how much revenue the measure would plausibly bring in and whether it would actually be one-time or recur.

I'm weighing the fiscal side: the LAO sees a modest income-tax loss and Stanford projects a negative effect, while the net revenue over five years looks plausibly positive but the long-run picture is uncertain. I'm now turning to the legal risk, where the retroactivity and residency provisions could be struck or narrowed, and the Tax Foundation sees a serious challenge ahead.

I'm now weighing the policy design: some features look sound, like the anti-avoidance rules, deferral options, and the non-supplant requirement, while others are more contestable, such as the constitutional entrenchment, the exemptions from the school guarantee and reserve rules, and the valuation method that uses 7.5 times book profits. The good-government concerns overlap with SPUR's position.

I'm weighing the political side now: the measure has appeal among some voters, but a broad coalition opposes it, including many Democrats, labor groups, and the Governor. I'm also noting that if Prop 40 passes, Props 41 or 42 could nullify it if they draw more yes votes, so a Yes vote could end up largely symbolic.

I'm leaning toward "No," since the money is uncertain and temporary while the legal, migration, and governance risks are real and the constitutional changes would be hard to reverse. Then there's the other view: that entrenching the measure in the constitution is itself a feature, not a bug.

I'm settling on a "No" lean as a defensible answer for a typical voter, while being careful that this is a judgment about risk tolerance and values rather than a verdict I should impose. The user asked for a direct call, so I'll give one and flag that it reflects how I weigh the uncertain money against the legal and governance risks.

I'm weighing whether "No" really is the right call or whether "Yes" holds up better. The strongest case for a generic voter is that this is a one-time 5% tax on roughly 250 very wealthy people, with revenue that could be large enough to offset federal Medi-Cal cuts.

I'm weighing the downside case more carefully now: the LAO puts the income-tax loss at under $1B a year, which is a small slice of a roughly $250B general fund, and the departures that would cause it are speculative. The legal risk is real, but the revenue would likely survive at least in part, and the one-time structure means it isn't a permanent middle-class tax, so for someone who prioritizes health coverage and fairness, "Yes" looks strong.

I'm weighing "No" against "Yes" here, since both are defensible and it comes down to how much weight I give the uncertain, temporary revenue versus the legal and governance risks. I'll give a direct call but make clear it reflects a judgment about risk and values, not a settled fact.

I'm weighing whether to give a single word at all, since a yes-or-no answer on a values-driven measure can hide real uncertainty, though the user asked for a direct call. Looking at the evidence, the central numbers are contested: estimated revenue ranges from about $30B to over $100B, and the net fiscal effect ranges from negative to positive, so a friend would likely say "No, but it's close" or "Yes, the fiscal risks look overstated," depending on how they weigh the risks.

I'm weighing the LAO's view, which puts the income-tax loss well below the revenue gain, against Hoover's more negative projection. The LAO is the official nonpartisan baseline, so its near-term positive read counts for a lot on fiscal grounds, even though the measure's one-time structure cuts both ways.

I'm now sizing the upside: the revenue could plausibly land somewhere around $50 to $90 billion if the measure mostly survives, with most of it going to health care that would otherwise be lost to federal cuts. That's a concrete benefit for millions of low-income Californians, which pulls against the legal and fiscal risks I was weighing.

I'm weighing the upside against the costs here: the fairness case for taxing about 250 very wealthy residents at a one-time 5% rate, plus anti-avoidance rules that keep the burden from recurring. On the other side, legal challenges could delay the money or strike parts of it, and the income-tax losses from departures, roughly $0.6 to $3.5 billion a year by various estimates, along with the reputational concern, are the costs I need to size.

I'm now checking the school funding piece: the Prop 98 exemption could leave K-14 with less than the normal formula would give, and the opponents' $3B-a-year figure would be a large cost if it holds, so I want to work out how much of that is real.

I'm checking how the Prop 98 exemption plays out against the opponents' roughly $3 billion a year figure, since the in-theory gap between the formula and the measure's education share is much smaller than that number suggests.

I'm working through the Prop 98 question: schools could end up with less than the normal formula would give. The rough math suggests a net shortfall for K-14, though the opponents' $3 billion figure may rest on different assumptions, so I'll present it as their estimate rather than settled fact.

I'm still working through the trade-offs here: the fiscal risk is contested, the benefit is real but temporary, and the structural federal cuts go unaddressed. I'll give a recommendation, but I need to be clear that it's a judgment about risk and values rather than something the evidence settles.

I'm now weighing the risk-of-harm angle: a one-time measure that leans on legal and behavioral bets for temporary money, with spending exemptions that blunt accountability, points toward "No." Yet the LAO's near-term fiscal read favors "Yes," so that pulls the other way.

I'm weighing the reversibility point now: if the measure passes and gets struck down or proves flawed, unwinding it would be hard, especially where the Prop 98 exemption and other provisions are written into the constitution. Against that, forgoing the revenue leaves health care exposed to federal cuts, and the legislature could still pursue other revenue options next session, which tilts me toward keeping the status quo.

I'm reconsidering whether "Yes" might be the better call, since the LAO's fiscal read and the measure's safeguards are fairly strong. Still, I'm keeping "No" as my lean: a "No" leaves room for other policy next session, while a "Yes" locks in constitutional commitments that would be hard to undo.

I'm checking the revenue range now: the Blue Sky model puts it at $76 to $151 billion even under adverse assumptions, while Hoover's $30 billion figure assumes a heavy litigation haircut. The LAO's "tens of billions" sits in between, so a midpoint around $60 billion looks reasonable.

Running the numbers on lost income tax against the one-time revenue, the net still looks positive under most central assumptions. I'm checking what happens if the revenue comes in closer to Hoover's $30 billion case.

I'm seeing that a "Yes" is not an unreasonable read: if the measure mostly survives, the expected net fiscal effect looks positive, and only large departures combined with heavy litigation losses would flip it negative. The case for "No" rests more on risk preferences, constitutional entrenchment, and precedent, since the lack of a permanent fix is true of any one-time revenue but not a special knock against this measure.

I'm weighing whether the measure's near-term fiscal benefit outweighs its risks, and the answer seems to hinge on whether the revenue is a real bridge. The federal cuts hit now, while any structural fix is a separate and harder political question, and the state's budget is in structural deficit regardless. For someone who thinks wealthy residents should pay more and that the health-care gap is urgent, "Yes" is a defensible choice; for someone wary of new taxes and of carving exemptions out of constitutional safeguards, "No" is equally defensible.

I'm weighing whether to give a flat yes or no when the evidence is close and the answer depends on how much weight someone puts on risk and constitutional entrenchment versus immediate health-care funding. The strongest flaw I see is that the high revenue estimates lean on assumptions about litigation and departures that could easily be wrong, so I can't treat them as settled.

I'm now looking at the arguments against the measure: the Yes side's "$100B" figure comes from its sponsors and goes beyond the LAO's "tens of billions," and its claim that billionaire flight is an overblown myth is contested. The No side has its own overstatements, like the $25B and $39B loss figures that assume lasting departures and ignore future revenue.

I'm weighing the honesty of both sides' figures: each camp overstates in places, and the nonpartisan sources read the measure as a risky bridge rather than a clear win or disaster. That makes the choice mostly a matter of values, so I'm considering how to frame it around whether a one-time tax on roughly 250 billionaires is worth the risk to fund health care now.

I'm settling on the reasoning for "No": when a measure would amend the constitution and carve out school funding guarantees, that's hard to reverse, while the revenue it promises is uncertain. Caution about constitutional changes and novel taxes is a principled default when the evidence stays this close.

I'm weighing whether a clear "No" is justified here, since the measure's revenue is one-time and uncertain while it would make lasting constitutional changes. Yet if the health care gap is urgent enough to justify that trade, a "Yes" follows, so I'm settling the answer on which of those two priorities I'd hold more firmly.

I'm checking the constitutional language now: the measure says it applies notwithstanding other provisions and exempts its revenue from several limits, including the Prop 98 school guarantee, so it's a real constitutional amendment, not just a tax.

I'm checking that the constitutional amendment makes the Sec 37(a) "one-time" language binding, so any future expansion would need voter approval, though the statutory part could be changed by a two-thirds vote. I'm weighing whether uncertainty about the revenue and legal outcomes is enough reason to vote no on a novel tax and constitutional change, or whether the status quo's certain federal cuts argue the other way.

I'm leaning toward "No," since the revenue is one-time and uncertain while the measure locks in constitutional changes that are hard to reverse. The Legislature could still pursue other revenue next session, though that isn't guaranteed. I'll stick with "No," stating the reasoning and the condition under which "Yes" would make sense.

Next I'm checking the measure's key practical details: the tax would be due in 2027 and could be paid in full or in five installments with a deferral charge, it would reach roughly 200 to 260 billionaires living in California, and net worth would be valued as of late 2026 using worldwide assets, minus directly held real estate and certain retirement accounts. I also note that about 90% of the revenue goes to health care and the rest to education and food programs.

I'm checking the remaining measure details now: it would be exempt from Prop 98, Prop 2, and Gann limits, the Legislature could amend it by a two-thirds vote if the changes match its purpose, and Props 41 and 42 could override it if they get more votes. I'm also noting the polling, which shows the measure trailing narrowly, and the spending gap between opponents and supporters.

I'm checking the figures the measure's sponsors and opponents cite: the Medi-Cal losses of up to $19B a year and the 1.3 million projected disenrollments both line up with the LAO's estimates, which makes them useful for weighing the health-care stakes.

I'm checking the Hoover paper's assumption that departing billionaires' income tax is lost for good, along with its $3.3–5.8B a year state income tax estimate, and I'm comparing that against the $3.2B a year average from Boll, Saez and Zucman for 2023–2025.

I'm weighing the Swiss evidence on reported wealth, which suggests that a wealth tax can shrink the base through mobility and valuation changes, and that could make the measure's assumed avoidance rate look optimistic.

I'm weighing the Swiss evidence against this measure's design: its effective rate works out to about 1% a year for five years, so the base erosion from mobility and valuation changes could be far larger than the 10% avoidance the Berkeley estimate assumes.

I'm working out how much the Swiss semi-elasticity would matter here: a 1 percentage point rate change there moved reported wealth by about 43%, which, if it carried over, would imply a far larger base erosion than the 10% avoidance the Berkeley estimate assumes. I still need to check whether that comparison holds, since the Swiss case used ongoing annual taxes and cantonal variation that this one-time measure doesn't share.

I'm checking the arithmetic on the Independent Institute's semi-elasticity: a 10% base reduction at a 5% rate works out to about 2% per percentage point, which is much lower than the Swiss estimates.

Checking the Independent Institute's figure against the Swiss estimates: a 10% base reduction at a 5% rate comes to roughly 2% per percentage point, far below the 43–100% Swiss range. That gap makes the Berkeley avoidance assumption look optimistic, though the Swiss cases involve annual taxes and cantonal variation that a one-time levy doesn't share.

The Swiss figures may overstate evasion here, since most of California's billionaire wealth sits in publicly traded stock that is hard to hide. The Berkeley 10% avoidance assumption still looks low, but the gap depends on how much of the base is private.

I'm weighing the LAO's nonpartisan estimate of under $1 billion a year in lost income tax against the sponsors' much higher figure, and noting that the Swiss evidence on mobility is only partly relevant because California's billionaire wealth is mostly publicly traded stock that is hard to hide.

I'm settling on the research picture: the LAO's nonpartisan view of tens of billions in revenue sits between the sponsors' higher estimate and the opponents' lower one, with a wide range and real downside risk. I'll weigh that range against the one-time, uncertain revenue and the constitutional changes that would be hard to undo.

I'm double-checking the measure's conflict rules: Props 41 and 42 would each nullify Prop 40 if they get more yes votes, and the official summaries describe them as voiding later-enacted taxes that conflict with this one.

I'm also weighing the spending gap, with opponents putting in more than $300 million against roughly $31 million from supporters.

I'm checking the measure's residency and timing rules: taxes are assessed on residency as of January 1, 2026, with valuation as of December 31, 2026, and worldwide assets count. I'm settling on a one-word answer, "No," and planning a few bullets of supporting evidence. I'll also say this is a values call where reasonable people disagree, and name the conditions under which someone should vote yes instead.

I'm now weighing the Prop 42 nuance: a Yes vote on Prop 40 only takes effect if it gets more yes votes than Props 41 and 42, and Prop 42 was actually ahead of it in late-October polling (51% vs. 46% yes). That matters for anyone voting yes, and it's the kind of detail I want to state clearly.

I'm settling on the shape of the answer: a one-word "No" up front, then a short rationale and the condition under which a Yes would make sense. I'll also note that this is a values call and that the research is current only through the pre-election coverage.

I'm thinking about how to present the answer: a one-word "No" up front, but I want to be clear it's my read of the evidence and that the decision is the user's, since this is a close call on values. I'm also considering whether to mention the risk that a one-time tax might turn into a recurring one, though the sponsors' stated preferences are a separate matter.

I'm weighing whether the Zucman point belongs in the answer at all: the measure text calls it a one-time tax, but he's on record preferring an annual one, and the two-thirds amendment clause could let later lawmakers expand it.

I'm working out the Medi-Cal bridge math: the measure's health account could hold up to about $22.5 billion a year, which is roughly what the federal cuts could take out of the state budget, so the revenue would cover those losses for a few years at most.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
**No.**

It's a values call, but the evidence on this measure leans toward no. A yes locks in constitutional changes and a legally contested tax for revenue that is uncertain and temporary.

- **Revenue is very uncertain.** Backers estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions." Hoover Institution economists estimate about $30 billion after departures and a litigation discount, and a net loss over time. Most of the gap comes from assumptions about court outcomes and departures.
- **It's a bridge, not a fix.** The measure's own findings put federal Medi-Cal losses at up to $19 billion a year, and state budget deficits are projected at $20–35 billion a year. At $30–100 billion total, the money covers roughly 1.5 to 5 years of federal losses.
- **It writes exemptions into the constitution.** The revenue is exempt from the school funding guarantee (Prop 98), the spending limit, and rainy-day rules. The nonpartisan Budget Center says schools would get less than if the money were ordinary General Fund revenue. Undoing this would take another statewide vote. The Legislature can also amend the statute by a two-thirds vote if the change is "consistent with and furthers" the measure's purposes.
- **Legal and migration risks are real.** The Tax Foundation calls the retroactive residency date fatally flawed. The drafters say facial challenges are weak. Either way, expect years of litigation. The LAO puts lost income tax from departures under $1 billion a year; Hoover puts it at $1–3.5 billion.

If you vote yes, note two things. Props 41 and 42 each cancel Prop 40 if they get more yes votes than it does. In PPIC's late-October poll, Prop 42 led Prop 40, 51% to 46% yes. Prop 40 also trailed in late polls (PPIC 46–52, Berkeley IGS 42–50).

Vote yes instead if you think the Medi-Cal gap is urgent enough to justify this risk. The federal cuts are real (the administration projects 1.3 million Medi-Cal disenrollments through 2029–30), and opponents haven't offered a funded replacement. You'd also need to expect courts to uphold most of the tax.

*Based on the official measure text, LAO and Budget Center analyses, PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, and coverage through Nov. 3, 2026.*

content.text:
**No.**

It's a values call, but the evidence on this measure leans toward no. A yes locks in constitutional changes and a legally contested tax for revenue that is uncertain and temporary.

- **Revenue is very uncertain.** Backers estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions." Hoover Institution economists estimate about $30 billion after departures and a litigation discount, and a net loss over time. Most of the gap comes from assumptions about court outcomes and departures.
- **It's a bridge, not a fix.** The measure's own findings put federal Medi-Cal losses at up to $19 billion a year, and state budget deficits are projected at $20–35 billion a year. At $30–100 billion total, the money covers roughly 1.5 to 5 years of federal losses.
- **It writes exemptions into the constitution.** The revenue is exempt from the school funding guarantee (Prop 98), the spending limit, and rainy-day rules. The nonpartisan Budget Center says schools would get less than if the money were ordinary General Fund revenue. Undoing this would take another statewide vote. The Legislature can also amend the statute by a two-thirds vote if the change is "consistent with and furthers" the measure's purposes.
- **Legal and migration risks are real.** The Tax Foundation calls the retroactive residency date fatally flawed. The drafters say facial challenges are weak. Either way, expect years of litigation. The LAO puts lost income tax from departures under $1 billion a year; Hoover puts it at $1–3.5 billion.

If you vote yes, note two things. Props 41 and 42 each cancel Prop 40 if they get more yes votes than it does. In PPIC's late-October poll, Prop 42 led Prop 40, 51% to 46% yes. Prop 40 also trailed in late polls (PPIC 46–52, Berkeley IGS 42–50).

Vote yes instead if you think the Medi-Cal gap is urgent enough to justify this risk. The federal cuts are real (the administration projects 1.3 million Medi-Cal disenrollments through 2029–30), and opponents haven't offered a funded replacement. You'd also need to expect courts to uphold most of the tax.

*Based on the official measure text, LAO and Budget Center analyses, PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, and coverage through Nov. 3, 2026.*

**No.**

It's a values call, but the evidence on this measure leans toward no. A yes locks in constitutional changes and a legally contested tax for revenue that is uncertain and temporary.

- **Revenue is very uncertain.** Backers estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions." Hoover Institution economists estimate about $30 billion after departures and a litigation discount, and a net loss over time. Most of the gap comes from assumptions about court outcomes and departures.
- **It's a bridge, not a fix.** The measure's own findings put federal Medi-Cal losses at up to $19 billion a year, and state budget deficits are projected at $20–35 billion a year. At $30–100 billion total, the money covers roughly 1.5 to 5 years of federal losses.
- **It writes exemptions into the constitution.** The revenue is exempt from the school funding guarantee (Prop 98), the spending limit, and rainy-day rules. The nonpartisan Budget Center says schools would get less than if the money were ordinary General Fund revenue. Undoing this would take another statewide vote. The Legislature can also amend the statute by a two-thirds vote if the change is "consistent with and furthers" the measure's purposes.
- **Legal and migration risks are real.** The Tax Foundation calls the retroactive residency date fatally flawed. The drafters say facial challenges are weak. Either way, expect years of litigation. The LAO puts lost income tax from departures under $1 billion a year; Hoover puts it at $1–3.5 billion.

If you vote yes, note two things. Props 41 and 42 each cancel Prop 40 if they get more yes votes than it does. In PPIC's late-October poll, Prop 42 led Prop 40, 51% to 46% yes. Prop 40 also trailed in late polls (PPIC 46–52, Berkeley IGS 42–50).

Vote yes instead if you think the Medi-Cal gap is urgent enough to justify this risk. The federal cuts are real (the administration projects 1.3 million Medi-Cal disenrollments through 2029–30), and opponents haven't offered a funded replacement. You'd also need to expect courts to uphold most of the tax.

*Based on the official measure text, LAO and Budget Center analyses, PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, and coverage through Nov. 3, 2026.*

CA
Prop
40
|
Constitutional Amendment and Statute
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
Enacts a one-time state wealth tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with a net worth of more than $1 billion.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors did not reach consensus on Prop. 40.
The proposed tax would provide one-time funds to meet the urgent health care and food access needs of millions of vulnerable Californians. Because it only applies to the wealthiest individuals with the most ability to pay, it is a progressive tax. However, the proposal fails on some good government principles. The tax’s one-time revenue would not fund ongoing health care and food programs. The state will need a permanent solution to the gaps H.R. 1 creates, not just a one-time fix. Furthermore, it could cost the state hundreds of millions in long-term revenue if billionaires flee in response. Prop. 40 has failed to gain consensus among many unions and health care advocates concerned about these potential negative impacts.
Given strong policy arguments for and against the measure, SPUR is not making an endorsement.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 40 Would Do
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time excise tax of 5% on individuals with a net worth of at least $1.1 billion in 2027. For individuals or trusts with a net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would decrease by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million in net worth below $1.1 billion. 1 The net worth calculation would include publicly traded securities, private business entities, art, intellectual property, vehicles, personal property, grantor trust assets, and dependents’ assets that exceed $50,000. The tax would not apply to real estate, pensions, individual retirement savings, and Roth accounts with an aggregate value below $10 million. Taxpayers could spread their payments over five years, but they would have to pay more to do so.
The tax would apply to all billionaires with residence in California on or after January 1, 2026. Because the date is retroactive, it may be challenging for some taxpayers to evade it by moving.
For many billionaires, their sources of wealth include publicly traded stocks as well as shares of private companies. The tax measure would value public stock at market price as of December 31, 2026, and value private business entities based on book value, estimated profits, and percentage of ownership or voting rights. Taxpayers could appeal the methodology and submit their own appraisals of private assets, including privately owned businesses, art, and intellectual property.
Revenues from Prop. 40 would be restricted. The vast majority of the funds, 90%, would go to health care to address recent federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal and other social programs. The remaining 10% would go to food assistance and education programs. Prop. 40 would prohibit the state from cutting existing funding for these purposes.
Prop. 40 includes language exempting its revenues from the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 2 Because a 5% tax on California’s billionaires would most likely push state revenues over the Gann Limit, this exemption would be critical to directing all of Prop. 40’s revenues to healthcare and food assistance.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenues. However, the exact amount is difficult to calculate because net worth fluctuates and some billionaires may find ways to reduce their liability.
The Backstory
Federal bill H.R. 1, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” was enacted in July 2025 and will make heavy cuts to critical social safety net programs across the state, including about $19 billion in annual funding losses to Medi-Cal. Medi-Cal covers more than one-third of the state’s population, including half of children aged 0 to 5, and nearly 15 million low-income Californians. 3 Funding cuts are projected to accelerate hospital closures across California, particularly in rural areas. They are also expected to heavily impact food assistance programs such as CalFresh and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which serve an estimated 5 million Californians.
The funding cuts are occurring as income inequality in California is increasing. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the highest-income families in the 90th percentile earn 11 times as much as the lowest-income families in the 10th percentile. 4 In recent years, inflation has hit low-income families the hardest, and households are struggling to pay for essential goods and services such as food, housing, transportation, and health care. 5
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country, with the highest income brackets paying the highest effective tax rates. In 2012, voters approved Prop. 30, which implemented tax rate increases on high-income earners, starting at $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for married couples. Voters renewed this income tax structure with Prop. 55 in 2016, extending it to 2030. (This election’s California Prop. 3 would make that increase permanent.) Despite concerns that tax rate increases cause wealthy Californians to leave the state, studies have shown no evidence of such tax flight following previous income tax increases. Indeed, the state has lost lower-income and less-educated adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults. 6
SEIU-UHW, a public sector union representing health care workers, placed Prop. 40 on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort. The measure requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 40 would be a highly progressive tax, applying only to individuals with more than $1 billion in net worth. California’s nearly 250 billionaires hold more than $2 trillion in wealth, up 48% from 2025 to 2026. Yet billionaires pay about 24% of their income in taxes, compared with 30% for the average taxpayer, and less than 1.5% of their wealth annually in federal, state, and local taxes. 7
Additionally, the measure would address disparities in how Californians experience the tax system. Low-income families bear a disproportionate burden from high housing costs and regressive taxes such as property and sales taxes, while inherited wealth is not taxed in California, contributing to income inequality and persistent racial wealth disparities. 8
The revenue raised would overwhelmingly support lower-income Californians by funding Medi-Cal, food assistance, and public education. These benefits have a racial equity dimension: According to U.S. Census data, low-income families in California are much more likely to be Latino or Black, while most high-income families are white or Asian. Prop. 40 would therefore raise revenue exclusively from the state’s wealthiest residents while directing it to services disproportionately relied on by lower-income, Black, and Latino Californians.
Pros
Implementing the proposed tax would generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue to mitigate the drastic federal funding cuts to healthcare, food assistance, and other services for low-income Californians, allowing many public and rural hospitals to remain open.
Revenues from the tax would disproportionately benefit low-income Californians who depend on Medi-Cal and SNAP benefits.
The highly progressive wealth tax would apply only to billionaires, who experienced enormous wealth gains last year. Because the tax is retroactive and one-time, it would be difficult for billionaires to evade.
Cons
Prop. 40 would fill a budget deficit with one-time funds and would not address the structural deficit left by federal funding cuts.
A potential exodus of billionaires in protest could reduce personal income tax revenue over time, a major ongoing source of state revenue.
California already has the highest income tax rate in the United States, and a new tax on private assets could strengthen the perception that the state is not a competitive location for individuals and companies.
No Recommendation

The latest article is dated Nov 3, 2026, so today is probably election day, and the vote on this measure is happening now or about to. SPUR, a nonpartisan urban policy group, said its board could not agree on Prop 40 and made no recommendation, which is worth noting even for an organization that generally favors more housing.

I'm noting that SPUR's board split and gave no recommendation, and that its concerns center on the measure's one-time funding and the risk of wealthy residents leaving. The Gann limit exemption is the key tension: proponents see it as necessary to direct all revenue to health care, while opponents say it skips the rebate and school allocation rules. That comes down to a values question.

I'm checking the Prop 41 and 42 polling against Prop 40, since a Yes vote on 40 could be nullified if either of those gets more yes votes. Props 41 and 42 both contain that nullification clause, and the late-October PPIC poll had Prop 42 ahead of Prop 40, which matters for a Yes voter.

Next I'm checking the expert critiques on the legal side: a Gupta Wessler risk assessment that rates facial challenges as low-risk, against the Tax Foundation's view that the measure faces many constitutional challenges and that its retroactive residency date is fatally flawed. I'm also noting Zucman's position that Prop 40 may be a first step toward an annual wealth tax, and the critique that Hoover's NPV estimates count the loss from fear of future taxes but not the gains.

I'm weighing the Medi-Cal angle now: the measure's health account can cover restoring federal cuts or protecting Medi-Cal, but the Legislature would decide how and when that money gets spent, so nothing guarantees it reaches Medi-Cal specifically.

I'm weighing the Legislature's room to amend the measure later: a two-thirds vote in each house could change it, and Democrats hold supermajorities in both chambers, though any amendment would still have to be consistent with and further the measure's purposes.

I'm checking whether Democrats really hold two-thirds of the seats in both houses, since that bears on how easily the Legislature could amend the measure later. **No.**

It's a values call, but the evidence on this measure leans toward no. A yes locks in constitutional changes and a legally contested tax for revenue that is uncertain and temporary.

- **Revenue is very uncertain.** Backers estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions." Hoover Institution economists estimate about $30 billion after departures and a litigation discount, and a net loss over time. Most of the gap comes from assumptions about court outcomes and departures.
- **It's a bridge, not a fix.** The measure's own findings put federal Medi-Cal losses at up to $19 billion a year, and state budget deficits are projected at $20–35 billion a year. At $30–100 billion total, the money covers roughly 1.5 to 5 years of federal losses.
- **It writes exemptions into the constitution.** The revenue is exempt from the school funding guarantee (Prop 98), the spending limit, and rainy-day rules. The nonpartisan Budget Center says schools would get less than if the money were ordinary General Fund revenue. Undoing this would take another statewide vote. The Legislature can also amend the statute by a two-thirds vote if the change is "consistent with and furthers" the measure's purposes.
- **Legal and migration risks are real.** The Tax Foundation calls the retroactive residency date fatally flawed. The drafters say facial challenges are weak. Either way, expect years of litigation. The LAO puts lost income tax from departures under $1 billion a year; Hoover puts it at $1–3.5 billion.

If you vote yes, note two things. Props 41 and 42 each cancel Prop 40 if they get more yes votes than it does. In PPIC's late-October poll, Prop 42 led Prop 40, 51% to 46% yes. Prop 40 also trailed in late polls (PPIC 46–52, Berkeley IGS 42–50).

Vote yes instead if you think the Medi-Cal gap is urgent enough to justify this risk. The federal cuts are real (the administration projects 1.3 million Medi-Cal disenrollments through 2029–30), and opponents haven't offered a funded replacement. You'd also need to expect courts to uphold most of the tax.

*Based on the official measure text, LAO and Budget Center analyses, PPIC and Berkeley IGS polls, and coverage through Nov. 3, 2026.*
